docs.title: Case schema
docs.text: This page lists every key a case YAML file may hold, with one example for each evaluator. evalkit lint checks a file against this schema. The machine-readable form is cases-v1.json, written by evalkit contracts export.

docs.title: File shapes
docs.text:
A case file is one of:

  • a single case (a mapping with id)
  • a list of cases and overlays (an overlay is an entry with extends)
  • a mapping with any of defaults, cases and overlays
defaults:
  tags: [balance-sheet]
  input: {company: acme}
  max_response_time: 90
cases:
  - id: acme-total-assets-fy2024
    input:
      question: What were Acme's total assets as of 31 March 2024?
    evaluators:
      output:
        answer_rubrics:
          rubrics:
            - rubric: Total assets as of 31 March 2024 are $4.2 billion.
              type: factual_retrieval

defaults takes only input, tags, max_response_time and agents (for overlays). A case's own input keys and max_response_time win over the defaults; tags are merged.

In the mapping shape, a top-level key starting with x- (for example x-shared) is ignored. Use it to hold YAML anchors that several cases reuse with *name.

docs.title: Case keys
docs.text: Key Type Meaning id string, required The case's identity, shared by every workspace. tags list of strings Labels for evalkit run --tag. The case's folder in the suite is added as a tag too. input mapping Sent to the agent as is. It must pass the agent's input schema; see Input schema. fixtures list of strings Keys from fixtures.yaml to attach as files. expected mapping Free-form ground truth, passed to custom evaluators. evaluators mapping Which evaluators score this case. See below.

docs.title: Input schema
docs.text:
Every agent has an input schema, a JSON Schema each case's input must pass. evalkit run, run_experiment (dry runs too) and evalkit lint --agent refuse inputs that fail it. When the agent sets none, the default applies:

{"type": "object", "required": ["question"], "properties": {"question": {"type": "string"}}}

A harness declares its own input_schema in GET /capabilities (Harness API). A code-driven agent stores one on the agent: evalkit agents create <name> --input-schema schema.json, or evalkit agents edit <name> --input-schema schema.json; --clear-input-schema goes back to the default. evalkit agents show prints it. For a multi-turn agent:

{"type": "object", "required": ["turns"], "properties": {"turns": {"type": "array", "items": {"type": "string"}}}}

docs.title: Evaluators
docs.text:
Evaluators sit under evaluators.output, evaluators.trajectory or evaluators.custom. The scorecard groups their scores into buckets, but the bucket names are not YAML keys:

Scorecard bucket YAML key content evaluators.output.answer_rubrics presentation evaluators.output.presentation_judge efficiency evaluators.output.max_response_time trajectory evaluators.trajectory.trajectory_rubrics, evaluators.trajectory.tool_trajectory_match, evaluators.trajectory.required_tools_called custom evaluators.custom.<name>

docs.title: answer_rubrics
docs.text:
What a correct answer contains. The judge marks each rubric satisfied, incorrect or absent.

evaluators:
  output:
    answer_rubrics:
      rubrics:
        - rubric: Revenue for FY2024 is $3.52 billion.
          type: factual_retrieval        # or derived_computation, analysis_interpretation
          source: the FY2024 annual report  # optional, factual_retrieval only
        - rubric: Revenue grew 12% from FY2023 to FY2024.
          type: derived_computation

Write one assertion per rubric. A rubric that bundles two ("states $300/month and explains why") fails as a whole when the answer gets only one part right, so a correct answer can be marked wrong. Split it into two rubrics.

docs.title: presentation_judge
docs.text:
How the answer shows its content: units, columns, an artifact relayed rather than restated. Each entry has exactly one of rubric (a property the answer must have) or forbid (a property it must not have). At least one entry must be a rubric.

evaluators:
  output:
    presentation_judge:
      rubrics:
        - rubric: A store count for each fiscal year FY2021–FY2025, as a table or a labelled list.
          points: 2      # optional weight, 1–10, default 1
        - forbid: Figures given without a currency unit.
          note: Rupee or dollar both fine.   # optional, shown to the judge

docs.title: max_response_time
docs.text:
A cap on the run's wall-clock time, in seconds. The value is a mapping, not a bare number. Only defaults.max_response_time also takes a bare number.

evaluators:
  output:
    max_response_time:
      max_seconds: 90

docs.title: trajectory_rubrics
docs.text:
Checkpoints the trajectory must show, one sentence each. Order is not graded.

evaluators:
  trajectory:
    trajectory_rubrics:
      rubrics:
        - Retrieves FY2024 Platform revenue as $3,522,776,000.
        - Rounds the final figure to the nearest basis point.

docs.title: tool_trajectory_match
docs.text:
Expected tool calls, matched by name and args. Tool names must match the trajectory exactly. The score is the share of expected calls found; ordered: true also requires them in this order.

evaluators:
  trajectory:
    tool_trajectory_match:
      ordered: false
      expected:
        - name: get_financials
          args: {ticker: ACME, period: FY2024}
          args_mode: subset    # subset, exact, ignore or substring
          match_overrides:     # optional, per arg: equals or substring
            period: substring

docs.title: required_tools_called
docs.text:
Tools the agent must call at least once. The score is the share called.

evaluators:
  trajectory:
    required_tools_called:
      tools: [get_financials, search_filings]

docs.title: custom
docs.text:
Remote evaluators and Python evaluators, keyed by their name. The block is passed to the evaluator as config, untouched.

evaluators:
  custom:
    sql_matches:
      table: revenue

docs.title: Python evaluators
docs.text:
A Python evaluator receives an EvalCase and an EvalRun and returns a float, a ScoreItem or a list of them. All three import from evalkit.sdk.

from evalkit.sdk import EvalCase, EvalRun, ScoreItem, evaluator


@evaluator(name="sql_matches")
def sql_matches(case: EvalCase, run: EvalRun) -> ScoreItem:
    table = case.config["table"]
    return ScoreItem(name="sql_matches", score=float(table in run.answer))
EvalCase field Meaning id Case id. input Case input, verbatim. expected The case's expected block, or None. config This evaluator's block from evaluators.custom. EvalRun field Meaning answer The final answer. A structured output as JSON text when the agent returned only that. output The structured output, or None. trajectory The ATIF trajectory as a dict.

ScoreItem has name, score (None means no reading), label and explanation.

docs.title: Overlays
docs.text:
An overlay adds evaluators to a case in another suite, for the agents it names. It may add tags, evaluators.custom and the tool_trajectory_match and required_tools_called trajectory evaluators.

overlays:
  - extends: acme-total-assets-fy2024
    agents: [support-bot]
    evaluators:
      trajectory:
        required_tools_called:
          tools: [get_financials]

docs.title: Sync cases from CI
docs.text:
Keep eval cases in your agent's repo and let CI put them on the server. A PR lints the cases; a merge to your default branch syncs them into a shared workspace, where reviewers approve them.

This page uses the dev and prod setup described in Example setup: personal → dev → prod: developers try cases in their personal workspaces, CI syncs merged cases into @dev, and approvals in @dev promote them to @prod. If your workspaces differ, change dev below to the workspace CI should sync into.

  • On every PR: evalkit lint <suite-dir> --dataset <suite>@dev fails the job on errors.
  • On merge: evalkit sync <suite-dir> --workspace dev writes the suite into <suite>@dev. The dataset name is the directory name.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• The server URL, as a CI variable EVALKIT_SERVER_URL (e.g. http://localhost:8020).
  • Credentials for a machine user. With single sign-on: a machine client at the identity provider (see Single sign-on), its id and secret as CI secrets EVALKIT_OIDC_CLIENT_ID and EVALKIT_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET, and an admin runs evalkit users add ci-bot --subject <sub> once and grants it writer on the workspace: evalkit workspaces members add dev ci-bot --role writer. Without single sign-on: a dedicated user with a password, created with evalkit users add ci-bot and granted writer the same way, with the password as a CI secret. Never the admin account.
  • A shared workspace to sync into, e.g. dev (see Workspaces).

Each job does three things:

  1. Installs the CLI at the server's version, so CI always runs the server's build.
  2. Authenticates as the machine user. Every server call needs a login, lint included.
  3. Runs evalkit lint or evalkit sync.

--actor is admin only. A machine user records itself as the actor, and --actor needs an admin machine user, which users promote refuses, so the case changelog shows ci-bot for a sync from CI. Where an admin does pass --actor, it is a free-text label: the server stores it as given and does not look it up among evalkit users.

Pass values from the commit through env:. Never write ${{ ... }} straight into a run: script: whoever pushes the commit controls those values, and the job holds the machine user's credentials.

docs.title: GitHub Actions example
docs.text:
The cases live in eval-cases/<suite>/. Change the paths and the workspace to match your repo.

name: eval cases
on:
  pull_request:
    paths: ["eval-cases/**"]
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths: ["eval-cases/**"]

env:
  EVALKIT_SERVER_URL: ${{ vars.EVALKIT_SERVER_URL }}

jobs:
  evalkit:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    env:
      EVALKIT_OIDC_CLIENT_ID: ${{ secrets.EVALKIT_OIDC_CLIENT_ID }}
      EVALKIT_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET: ${{ secrets.EVALKIT_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@v6
      - name: Install the evalkit CLI
        run: uv tool install --reinstall "evalkit-py==$(curl -fsSL "$EVALKIT_SERVER_URL/api/cli" | jq -r .version)"
      - name: Lint
        if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'
        run: |
          for suite in eval-cases/*/; do
            evalkit lint "$suite" --dataset "$(basename "$suite")@dev"
          done
      - name: Sync
        if: github.event_name == 'push'
        run: |
          for suite in eval-cases/*/; do
            evalkit sync "$suite" --workspace dev
          done

Without single sign-on, keep a Log in step: evalkit login --url "$EVALKIT_SERVER_URL" --username ci-bot --password "$EVALKIT_CI_PASSWORD".

The same steps work in any CI: install, authenticate, lint or sync.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Sync reads the git branch and sha itself. Pass --version and --branch when the checkout has no git history.
  • Sync uploads any fixture bytes the server does not hold yet. Set fixtures: in evalkit.yaml if your cases use fixtures (see Config).
  • A full suite sync removes cases that are no longer on disk. Experiments that already ran keep the case versions they used.
  • --dataset on lint lets the server check case ids and overlay targets against the other datasets. Without it, those checks only run at sync.
  • If dev is linked to prod for promotion, sync only into dev. prod refuses sync; approved cases reach it through promotion.
  • Synced cases start Unreviewed. Reviewers of the workspace approve them; see the Quickstart.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
The words you need before your first scorecard. Everything else is explained on the page that uses it.

Term Meaning Case One eval question, written in YAML: the input, the rubrics a right answer meets, and the checks to run. Dataset A directory of cases, run and tracked together. The directory name is the dataset name, and subfolders become tags you can run alone. Sync Copying a dataset directory to the server. Runs do it for you. Workspace Where datasets, agents and experiments live: your own (named after you), or a shared one such as dev. Every user can read every workspace; only the owner changes a personal one, and admins and writers change a shared one. Reference name@workspace, for example acme@dev. A bare name means your own workspace. Agent Your agent, registered once on the server. A code-driven agent is run by your own code; this is the usual way to start. Task The function run_experiment calls once per case. It calls your agent and returns the answer. Experiment One run of a dataset against an agent. Run One case answered once. Single sign-on Signing in through your organisation's identity provider. The first sign-in creates your evalkit user. See Single sign-on. Subject The stable id your identity provider assigns you; evalkit keys your user on it, not on your email. Machine user A user bound to a machine client at the identity provider, for CI. No password, no browser. evalkit users add <name> --subject <sub>. Trace, span, session What your agent records as it works: one span per model call or tool call. One run is one session. Mapping Which span attribute holds the model, the messages, the tokens and each tool call. Trajectory The step-by-step record of a run that evalkit builds from the spans. Judge The LLM that grades an answer against the case's rubrics. By default it runs on the evalkit server, served by an LLM provider configured there; you can bring your own key instead. Evaluator One scoring check, for example the rubric check or "did the agent call this tool". Scorecard The table of scores for an experiment, per case and per bucket (content, trajectory, presentation, efficiency, custom). Case schema maps each bucket to its YAML key, e.g. presentation → evaluators.output.presentation_judge. Unreviewed A case in a shared dataset with no review decision at its current content. It runs like any other case; review decides promotion. Promotion An admin links a shared workspace to a target (evalkit workspaces promote-to dev prod). Approving a case in dev adds it, approved, to the same-named dataset in prod. Datasets in prod are fed only that way. evalkit.yaml The file in your repo that says where your cases are and which environment variables hold API keys.

Next: Try locally to see these on a running server, or the Quickstart to connect your own agent.

docs.title: Config: evalkit.yaml
docs.text:
evalkit.yaml sits at the root of the repository that holds your eval cases or your agent. The CLI and the SDK look for it above the current directory. It names the case and fixture directories and the API keys the runs from this machine use.

cases: eval/cases # optional: directory whose children are datasets
fixtures: eval/fixtures # optional: fixture bytes, flat, keyed by filename

credentials: # values are env:NAME, read when a run needs them
  agents:
    myagent: env:MYAGENT_KEY # a bare name means your own workspace
  evaluators:
    citation_check: env:EVALUATOR_KEY

Only your personal Harness API agents use credentials.agents here. The server drives shared agents (ouragent@dev) with the keys stored in its database, so an entry for one in evalkit.yaml is never read. The same holds for shared remote evaluators.

Put the values in a .env file next to evalkit.yaml (and keep it out of git), or in your shell. A variable set in the shell wins over .env.

Agents, remote evaluators and the judge are not configured here:

  • Agents are created once on the server with evalkit agents create (or on the Agents page). A personal agent runs from your machine; a shared one is driven by the server. An agent without a harness URL is code-driven: only run_experiment can run it. See SDK runs.
  • Remote evaluators are created with evalkit evaluators create. A run uses the evaluators in its agent's workspace.
  • The judge of an experiment is the server's default judge (an admin sets it with evalkit judge-default set) unless you pick one. Re-evaluating an experiment always reuses its judge. You pick it in one of two ways:
  • An LLM provider configured on the server: evalkit run … --judge-provider NAME --judge-model M, or run_experiment(judge=Judge(provider=..., model=...)). The default judge is one too. The evaluators that use a judge (answer_rubrics, presentation_judge, trajectory_rubrics) then run on the evalkit server with its stored key, so you need no judge key on your machine.
  • Your own judge: evalkit run … --judge-base-url URL --judge-model M --judge-api-key-env NAME, where NAME is the env var (or .env entry) holding the key; or run_experiment(judge=Judge(base_url=..., model=..., api_key=...)). Those evaluators then run on your machine. The key goes only to your judge and is never stored on the evalkit server, so re-scoring and resuming ask for it again: evalkit evaluate <id> --judge-api-key-env NAME, evalkit run … --resume <id> --judge-api-key-env NAME, or evaluate_experiment(..., judge=Judge(base_url=..., model=..., api_key=...)), the same judge again. A different judge is refused.
  • --judge-provider and --judge-base-url together are refused, and so is --judge-base-url without --judge-api-key-env.

Rules:

  • env:NAME values are read only when a command needs them. A missing variable is an error that names it.
  • An agent or evaluator with no credentials entry is called without a key, and the run prints one line saying so.
  • credentials holds agent and evaluator keys only. A file with credentials.llm_providers (or the older credentials.judges) fails to load: pass your own judge's key with the run instead.
  • cases and fixtures are optional. Leave them out when you only run shared datasets, for example from run_experiment. Commands that need them say so:
  • evalkit sync <name> and evalkit run <name> on a dataset in your workspace need cases to find <cases>/<name>. Passing the dataset's directory instead (evalkit sync eval/cases/finance) works without it.
  • A sync uploads fixture bytes from fixtures. Without it, a case whose fixture the server does not already hold fails the sync with E-FIXTURE-MISSING.
  • run_experiment on a dataset in your workspace skips the sync without cases and runs the copy the server holds.
  • Fixtures a run downloads go to fixtures, or to a temporary directory when it is not set.

docs.title: Framework mappings
docs.text:
Ready-to-use mappings for popular agent frameworks. Pick your framework, copy its file, and create the agent with it. Each one is the connect-traces skill's openinference.json or gen_ai.json plus a few changes, and ships beside them in the skill's references/ folder (evalkit skills install copies it to .claude/skills/connect-traces/references/ or .agents/skills/…).

cp .claude/skills/connect-traces/references/<framework>.json eval/span-mapping.json
evalkit agents create myagent --trajectory-source otel --mapping eval/span-mapping.json

Then run one session and check it with evalkit traces check myagent <session id> (see Tracing). Each line of the check output starts with ✓ (fine), ! (a warning: the check still exits 0, but the trajectory is likely wrong) or ✗ (a failure). Instrumentors change between versions, so read every warning line even when you start from a file below.

Framework Instrumentation File Verified with LangGraph OpenInference LangChain openinference.json LangGraph 1.2 LangChain create_agent OpenInference LangChain langchain.json LangChain 1.4 CrewAI OpenInference CrewAI + OpenAI crewai.json CrewAI 1.15 Agno OpenInference Agno agno.json Agno 3.1 OpenAI Agents SDK OpenInference openai-agents openinference.json openai-agents 0.24 LlamaIndex FunctionAgent OpenInference LlamaIndex llamaindex.json LlamaIndex 0.14 Google ADK ADK's own GenAI spans google-adk.json ADK 2.13 Pydantic AI built-in GenAI spans gen_ai.json Pydantic AI 2.65 Claude Agent SDK hand-built GenAI spans + the mcp library claude-agent-sdk.json claude-agent-sdk 0.2.177 Mastra (TypeScript) @mastra/otel-exporter GenAI spans mastra.json Mastra 1.81

Some fixes need a change in the agent, not the mapping: a mapping reads one span at a time and cannot move a session id or an output from one span to another. Each section says what the agent still needs.

docs.title: Every framework: a session id on each turn
docs.text:
Put the session id on the outermost span of each turn. Each span joins the session of its outermost ancestor that carries one, so a web framework's request span (FastAPI, Starlette) above it that has no session id does not matter. See Agent behind an HTTP server for the ways to stamp it.

When the agent runs inside the process that calls run_experiment, the SDK's evalkit.run span carries the session id and this is already done.

Tool spans from most OpenInference instrumentors carry no tool.id. The check then reports "0 matched to calls by id", and evalkit matches tool results to calls by time and order. That is expected; nothing to fix.

docs.title: LangGraph
docs.text:
openinference.json as it is.

  • A graph node named agent (the tutorial's default) is emitted as an AGENT span. If every model step shows up as a subagent, rename the node, or add "rekind_spans": [{"name": "agent", "kind": "chain"}].

docs.title: LangChain
docs.text:
langchain.json: openinference.json with input.value, output.value, llm.input_messages.* and llm.output_messages.* in known_attributes. LangChain's CHAIN spans carry flattened messages that the trajectory does not need.

  • Put the session id on a span of your own around each turn (see above).

docs.title: CrewAI
docs.text:
crewai.json: openinference.json with CrewAI's agent and tool attributes (agent.backstory, agent.goal, agent.tools, conversation.turn_index, tool.cache_function, tool.current_usage_count, tool.description_updated, tool.result_as_answer) in known_attributes.

  • Pass provider="openai" (or your provider) to the LLM, or the OpenAI instrumentor does not see the calls.
  • If you wrap each turn in your own span, give it kind CHAIN, not AGENT.

docs.title: Agno
docs.text:
agno.json: openinference.json with agno.* in known_attributes.

  • Set OTEL_SPAN_ATTRIBUTE_COUNT_LIMIT=4096. The default of 128 attributes per span drops the system prompt from the flattened messages. evalkit traces check warns on its llm line when a span lost attributes this way.

docs.title: OpenAI Agents SDK
docs.text:
openinference.json as it is.

  • Wrap each turn in OpenInference's using_session(session_id), so the agent's spans carry the session id.
  • The workflow trace is an AGENT span named after workflow_name. If the real agent shows up as a subagent of it, add "exclude_spans": ["<workflow name>"].

docs.title: LlamaIndex
docs.text:
llamaindex.json: openinference.json with input.value and output.value in known_attributes, and three rekind_spans rules. LlamaIndex emits three LLM-kind spans per model call (an empty _prepare_chat_with_tools span and an outer astream_chat span around the real one), each named after the LLM class (OpenAI.astream_chat, OpenAILike.astream_chat, …). The rules keep the astream_chat span that carries llm.finish_reason as the LLM call and make the other two chains, whatever the class:

"rekind_spans": [
  {"name": "*.astream_chat", "attribute": "llm.finish_reason", "kind": "llm"},
  {"name": "*.astream_chat", "kind": "chain"},
  {"name": "*._prepare_chat_with_tools", "kind": "chain"}
]
  • If traces check still shows more LLM spans than LLM steps, look up the extra span's name in --dump spans.json and add a rule for it.
  • For token counts on streamed calls, pass additional_kwargs={"stream_options": {"include_usage": True}} to the LLM.
  • Put the session id on a span of your own around each turn (see above).

docs.title: Google ADK
docs.text:
google-adk.json: gen_ai.json with "exclude_spans": ["execute_tool (merged)"] (ADK emits a merged copy of parallel tool calls) and ADK's own attributes (gcp.vertex.agent.*, input.value, output.value, session.id) in known_attributes.

  • Set OTEL_INSTRUMENTATION_GENAI_CAPTURE_MESSAGE_CONTENT=SPAN_ONLY. On ADK 2.13, true gives spans without messages.
  • Put the session id on a span of your own around each turn (see above), or create the app with FastAPI(telemetry={"tracing": False}).
  • ADK's execute_tool spans carry no gen_ai.conversation.id; they join the session through the turn span above them.

docs.title: Pydantic AI
docs.text:
gen_ai.json as it is.

  • Pydantic AI sets gen_ai.conversation.id to a new id per agent.run. Your turn span's session id wins over it (see above); passing agent.run(..., conversation_id=session_id) as well is optional and keeps the ids the same in other trace tools.
  • If you use Logfire, add the attributes traces check lists as unmapped to known_attributes.

docs.title: Claude Agent SDK
docs.text:
claude-agent-sdk.json: gen_ai.json with "exclude_spans": [{"scope": "mcp-python-sdk"}] and mcp.* and jsonrpc.* in known_attributes. The mcp library emits its own execute_tool spans for every tools/call, which would count each tool call twice. Excluded spans still report their attributes as unmapped, hence the known_attributes.

  • The SDK has no OTel instrumentation of its own; the agent builds GenAI spans by hand.
  • The SDK reports token usage per turn only: put the totals on the turn's last chat span.
  • Add your own app's attribute prefixes to known_attributes.

docs.title: Mastra
docs.text:
mastra.json: gen_ai.json with these changes:

  • exclude_spans drops Mastra's internal spans by mastra.span.type: processor_run, memory_operation and model_chunk.
  • answer is invoke_agent <agent name>.text. Replace <agent name> with your agent's name. If you don't, evalkit traces check warns on its answer line that no span has that name, and the trajectory has no answer. The rule splits on the first ., so this form does not work for an agent name with a dot in it; rename the agent or use root.
  • known_attributes adds mastra.*, gen_ai.usage.reasoning_tokens and gen_ai.tool.call.id.

Mastra's chat spans end without gen_ai.output.messages; the text and tool calls sit on the parent agent_step span, and a mapping cannot read a parent span. Wrap the exporter in a SpanExporter that copies mastra.model_step.output from each agent_step span onto its chat span.

Mastra is TypeScript and the SDK is Python: a Python task calls the agent over HTTP and passes metadata["session_id"] along, and the agent uses it as its session id (see SDK runs).

docs.title: Harness API
docs.text:
The Harness API is the HTTP contract a client's agent harness implements so evalkit can drive it: start a run, poll its status, serve its trajectory. Agents in a shared workspace are driven by this server; agents in a personal workspace by evalkit run from their owner's machine. The OpenAPI schema ships inside the CLI:

evalkit contracts export --target ./contracts   # harness-api-v1.json, atif-accepted.json, …

Each endpoint lets evalkit do one thing. Every Harness API has the first three; declare the rest in the capabilities response when you implement them. An agent on the SDK + traces path has no Harness API and none of these endpoints; evalkit sees what its task returns and the spans it exports.

Endpoint Lets evalkit Capability flag Without it GET /capabilities see what the harness supports and gate evaluators on it (snapshotted per experiment) part of every Harness API — POST /runs invoke the agent: start one run in a fresh session with the case input and files part of every Harness API — GET /runs/{id} wait for the run and read its answer, structured output, model and artifact list part of every Harness API — GET /runs/{id}/trajectory read the trajectory (ATIF): the run view, trajectory evaluators and token/cost gauges provides.trajectory trajectory evaluators skip, unless the agent's trajectory source is otel and the trajectory comes from spans GET /runs/{id}/files, GET /runs/{id}/files/{path} read the workspace: the run's Workspace tab, downloads and artifact copies provides.workspace no Workspace tab; artifacts the run reports are not copied GET /runs list the agent's sessions on the Runs page and for evalkit runs list/runs pull, including ones evalkit did not start; optional since/until filter by creation time provides.run_listing the Runs page is empty for this agent POST /runs/{id}/stop cancel a run that hit its time limit accepts.stop timed-out runs keep running on the harness

POST /runs takes JSON, or multipart when the case has fixture files and the harness accepts files but not file_urls. Run status moves through queued, running, then one of completed, failed, cancelled.

A code-driven agent (no harness_url) has none of these endpoints, so its runs have no Workspace tab. To see an agent's files in evalkit, give it a Harness API with at least the files endpoints; its trajectory can still come from traces.

Every request carries x-api-key. Two rules matter more than the rest:

  • Capabilities honesty. Declare only what works. evalkit neutral-skips evaluators whose inputs the harness does not provide; a false true produces failing scores blamed on the agent.
  • Implement stop. evalkit calls stop on timeout when accepts.stop is true; a harness without it leaks resources on every timed-out run.

docs.title: Input schema
docs.text:
Every case input must pass the agent's input schema; evalkit run and evalkit lint --agent refuse inputs that fail it. A harness declares its schema as input_schema in GET /capabilities:

{
  "agent": "support-bot",
  "input_schema": {
    "type": "object",
    "required": ["turns"],
    "properties": {"turns": {"type": "array", "items": {"type": "string"}}}
  },
  "check_input": {"turns": ["Hi. Reply with one word."]}
}

Without input_schema, the default applies: an object with a required string question. Declare check_input too when the default probe {"question": "Hi. Reply with one word."} does not pass your schema, so evalkit harness check can run. See Input schema.

docs.title: Already have a harness? Keep it
docs.text:
A harness that already emits OpenTelemetry traces can skip the trajectory endpoint: create the agent with --trajectory-source otel --mapping FILE and export spans to the collector with the run id it returned from POST /runs in the attribute the mapping's session_id rule names (session.id for OpenInference, gen_ai.conversation.id for GenAI). Everything else stays: server runs, evalkit run, the Workspace tab. The harness declares provides.trajectory: false. See Tracing.

The session evalkit polls is the run_id that POST /runs returns; there is no separate session field. A queue-backed agent whose worker opens its own session can return that session id as run_id, or stamp the run_id it returned on the job's spans in the mapping's session id attribute. Either way the ids must also work with the other /runs/{id} endpoints.

Moving to SDK runs instead only makes sense to stop hosting the harness. A code-driven agent loses server-started runs and the Workspace tab, and run_experiment refuses an agent with a harness_url: keep one agent name and run it with evalkit run, rather than adding a second entry for run_experiment.

docs.title: Checking
docs.text:
evalkit harness check ouragent@dev

runs a trivial call, exercises every declared capability and prints a pass/fail table. For a harness agent whose trajectory source is otel the trajectory row reads "from traces" and a session row reports the collected spans.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
evalkit is one Python package on PyPI, evalkit-py. It holds the evalkit command (the CLI), the evalkit.sdk module for SDK runs and, with the server extra, the server itself. It needs Python 3.12 or newer, for the CLI, the SDK and the server alike.

Your CLI and SDK must run the same version as the evalkit server you use: local runs and SDK runs refuse to start otherwise. The commands on this page pin version 0.4.0.dev72. On your server's own /docs/install page, that is the server's version; curl <server url>/api/cli prints it anywhere.

docs.title: The CLI, as a global tool
docs.text:
uv tool install --reinstall "evalkit-py==0.4.0.dev72"

With pipx instead: pipx install --force "evalkit-py==0.4.0.dev72".

curl http://localhost:8020/api/cli prints the server's version, for scripts and CI:

uv tool install --reinstall "evalkit-py==$(curl -fsSL http://localhost:8020/api/cli | jq -r .version)"

docs.title: The CLI, inside a project
docs.text:
To keep evalkit out of your global tools, add it to a uv project and run it with uv run. The CLI needs no extra; add otel if the same project uses tracing.register or SDK runs, and server if you also run the server from there:

uv add "evalkit-py==0.4.0.dev72"
uv run evalkit --help

If you give evalkit its own uv project in a folder of your agent's uv project (say eval/), create it with uv init --no-workspace:

cd eval && uv init --no-workspace && uv add "evalkit-py==0.4.0.dev72"

Without the flag, uv silently adds eval/ to your agent project's workspace, so it shares your agent's lockfile.

docs.title: The SDK, into a project
docs.text:
run_experiment and tracing.register live in the same package as the CLI. The otel extra brings the OpenTelemetry SDK and the OTLP exporter. Pin the server's version; uv.lock records it:

uv add "evalkit-py[otel]==0.4.0.dev72"

With pip instead: pip install "evalkit-py[otel]==0.4.0.dev72".

To keep evalkit out of the app's dependencies, run the eval script with it instead:

uv run --with "evalkit-py[otel]==0.4.0.dev72" python eval/run.py

docs.title: The server
docs.text:
uv tool install --reinstall "evalkit-py[server]==0.4.0.dev72" (or pip install "evalkit-py[server]==0.4.0.dev72") installs the server too: the API, the web UI and migrations. To run one on your machine against a Postgres you already have:

evalkit init-server   # creates the database, writes config.yaml and .env in ./evalkit-try
cd evalkit-try && evalkit serve

Try locally walks through it with a sample agent; Server config lists every config.yaml key; the evalkit-deployment skill covers running a server for a team.

docs.title: The skills
docs.text:
The skills teach a coding agent to write cases, connect traces and run evals. Copy them into your repo, from the repo root:

evalkit skills install

They go to .claude/skills/ when .claude/ exists, else .agents/skills/; --target DIR picks another directory. The user docs they link to go to evalkit-docs/ beside them. The connect-traces skill's starting span mappings land in connect-traces/references/ (openinference.json, gen_ai.json).

skills install also writes outside the repo: it appends the target directory to ~/.evalkit/skills-targets, so that evalkit update can refresh it later.

docs.title: Updating
docs.text:
Every API response carries X-Evalkit-Version. The CLI warns when it differs from the server and refuses when the major versions differ. Local runs and SDK runs refuse any difference, so after a server deploy, from the project's root:

evalkit update

It reinstalls the CLI at the server's version and, when pyproject.toml pins evalkit-py==…, moves the pin and runs uv sync. It then refreshes the skills in every directory evalkit skills install wrote to on this machine (listed in ~/.evalkit/skills-targets), and in ./.claude/skills or ./.agents/skills if they hold an earlier install; commit the changes in repos that track the skills. Pass --no-skills to skip that.

A CLI older than 0.3.0 cannot update itself: evalkit update fails with KeyError: 'filename'. Run the global tool install command once instead; evalkit update works from then on.

A project that vendored an evalkit wheel before evalkit was on PyPI moves to PyPI once: uv remove evalkit && uv add "evalkit-py[otel]==0.4.0.dev72".

Next: Login.

docs.title: Login
docs.text:
evalkit login --url http://localhost:8020

With single sign-on configured on the server, the command opens your browser at your identity provider. Sign in there; the browser comes back to the CLI on a local port, and the CLI stores the identity provider's tokens in ~/.evalkit/config.toml. They refresh themselves. On a machine without a browser, evalkit login --url http://localhost:8020 --no-browser prints a URL and a code to enter on any device.

Without single sign-on, or with --username, the command asks for a username and password and stores an evalkit token instead. With single sign-on configured, password login is for admins unless the deployer set password_login: all.

The CLI talks to one server at a time: logging in again, to the same server or another, replaces the stored login. Dev and prod are workspaces on one server (finance@dev, finance@prod), not separate logins.

evalkit whoami shows who the login is, its kind (sso, password or client credentials) and when the current token expires, and exits 1 if the server rejects it. An SSO access token expires within the hour and renews itself; that line is not a reason to log in again. When a command fails with your login has expired, run evalkit login again.

The first sign-in creates your evalkit user, named after the part before @ in your identity provider's username or email. If that name is taken, the command says so and names the subject an admin binds with evalkit users bind; see Single sign-on.

docs.title: Scripts and CI
docs.text:
Pipelines authenticate as a machine client at the identity provider:

export EVALKIT_SERVER_URL=http://localhost:8020
export EVALKIT_OIDC_CLIENT_ID=<client id>
export EVALKIT_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET=<client secret>

No evalkit login is needed; every command fetches a token itself. An admin binds the client once: see CI sync. Without single sign-on, EVALKIT_SERVER_URL and EVALKIT_TOKEN carry an evalkit token, or the job logs in with a dedicated non-admin password user.

docs.title: Timeout
docs.text:
The CLI and the SDK wait up to 120 seconds for each server call. Set EVALKIT_TIMEOUT (seconds) to wait longer, for example on a slow network:

export EVALKIT_TIMEOUT=300

It covers calls to the evalkit server only. The server's own calls to an agent's harness keep their fixed limits, and so does evalkit harness check.

The SDK uses the same login and the same variables. A deployed agent that only exports traces uses an agent token; see Tracing.

docs.title: Mappings
docs.text:
A mapping tells evalkit which span attribute holds each field of the evalkit span format (ESF): the span kind, the session id, the model, the messages, the token counts, the tool name and call id. It also says where the run's answer comes from (answer) and which spans to leave out (exclude_spans).

Every agent whose trajectories come from traces has its own mapping. evalkit agents create NAME --trajectory-source otel --mapping FILE makes the first version active. Start from the file for your framework in Framework mappings, or from the connect-traces skill's openinference.json or gen_ai.json, which cover agents on the OpenInference or GenAI semantic conventions as they are. Spans that reach an agent with no active mapping are stored without a session id.

An existing agent switches between ATIF and traces with evalkit agents edit NAME --trajectory-source otel --mapping FILE (or --trajectory-source atif), or from the agent's Edit dialog. Switching to traces without a file reuses the agent's last active mapping. The switch is refused while one of the agent's experiments is running, and experiments that already ran keep the source they ran with.

A mapping applies to every span of the agent and is versioned: evalkit traces mapping push creates a draft, you review the draft against recent sessions on the agent's Mappings tab (Agents → the agent → Mappings), and activate it there or with evalkit traces mapping activate. The connect-traces skill walks a coding agent through writing one.

docs.title: The document
docs.text:
{
  "schema_version": "1",
  "kind": {
    "attribute": "openinference.span.kind",
    "values": {
      "LLM": "llm",
      "TOOL": "tool",
      "AGENT": "agent",
      "CHAIN": "chain",
      "RETRIEVER": "retriever"
    }
  },
  "session_id": {
    "attribute": "session.id"
  },
  "model": {
    "attribute": "llm.model_name"
  },
  "input_messages": {
    "attribute": "llm.input_messages",
    "message_format": "openinference"
  },
  "output_messages": {
    "attribute": "llm.output_messages",
    "message_format": "openinference"
  },
  "tokens": {
    "prompt": {
      "attribute": "llm.token_count.prompt"
    },
    "completion": {
      "attribute": "llm.token_count.completion"
    },
    "cached": {
      "attribute": "llm.token_count.prompt_details.cache_read"
    },
    "cache_write": {
      "attribute": "llm.token_count.prompt_details.cache_write"
    }
  },
  "cost_usd": {
    "attribute": "llm.cost.total"
  },
  "tool": {
    "name": {
      "attribute": "tool.name"
    },
    "call_id": {
      "attribute": "tool.id"
    },
    "arguments": {
      "attribute": "input.value",
      "json": true
    },
    "result": {
      "attribute": "output.value"
    }
  },
  "agent_name": {
    "attribute": "agent.name"
  },
  "input": {
    "attribute": "input.value",
    "json": true
  },
  "output": {
    "attribute": "output.value",
    "json": true
  },
  "known_attributes": [
    "openinference.span.kind",
    "session.id",
    "user.id",
    "metadata",
    "tag.tags",
    "input.mime_type",
    "output.mime_type",
    "llm.provider",
    "llm.system",
    "llm.invocation_parameters",
    "llm.finish_reason",
    "llm.tools.*",
    "llm.token_count.total",
    "llm.token_count.prompt_details.*",
    "llm.token_count.completion_details.*",
    "llm.cost.*",
    "tool.description",
    "tool.parameters",
    "tool.json_schema",
    "agent.name",
    "graph.node.*"
  ]
}

That is the skill's openinference.json. Its gen_ai.json reads gen_ai.operation.name (chat, execute_tool, invoke_agent, …), gen_ai.request.model, gen_ai.input.messages / gen_ai.output.messages with "message_format": "gen_ai", gen_ai.usage.input_tokens and friends, reads the system prompt from gen_ai.system_instructions, cache writes from gen_ai.usage.cache_creation.input_tokens and the agent's name from gen_ai.agent.name, and sets "cost_usd": null because the conventions define no cost attribute. Both list the other attributes of their convention under known_attributes, so evalkit traces check does not report them as unmapped; entries may be exact keys or globs such as llm.tools.*.

Rule shapes:

Shape Result {"attribute": K} the attribute's value, or null {"attribute": K, "json": true} the value parsed as JSON when it is a string; the string stays when parsing fails {"attribute": K, "values": {...}} the value translated through the table; an unlisted kind becomes other {"attribute": K, "message_format": F} the messages laid out under K per format F: openinference (flattened indexed keys), gen_ai (JSON list of messages with parts), openai (JSON list of chat messages) null never read

More fields shape the trajectory:

  • answer: where the run's answer comes from: root, a span name, or <span name>.<output key>. Default root.
  • exclude_spans: spans left out of the trajectory. Default none.
  • rekind_spans: spans that get another kind than the kind rule gives, e.g. {"name": "agent", "kind": "chain"} for a graph node tagged AGENT that is only a step. The first match wins.
  • main_agent: the agent span whose answer and id the trajectory carries, when evalkit picks the wrong one. When it matches several spans (one per chat turn), the earliest gives the id and the latest the answer.
  • subagent_spans: agent spans to keep as subagent trajectories even though no tool span starts them.

Each entry is a span match:

Match Matches a span when "OpenAILike.*" its name matches the glob {"name": G} its name matches the glob G {"attribute": K} it has attribute K {"attribute": K, "equals": V} attribute K holds V, compared as text: 1, 1.0 and "1" match each other, and so do true and "true" {"scope": G} its instrumentation scope name (e.g. mcp) matches the glob G

An object match may give several of name, attribute and scope; every one given must match.

The span name alone is not always enough: two LLM spans with the same name, or spans that come from another library's instrumentation. Match on an attribute or the scope then.

Every mapping is complete on its own; there is no inheritance. The schema ships as span-mapping-v1.json with evalkit contracts export.

docs.title: The loop
docs.text:
evalkit traces check myagent <session id> --dump spans.json   # read the raw attributes
evalkit traces mapping push myagent eval/span-mapping.json    # upload a draft
evalkit traces check myagent <session id> --mapping draft     # preview with the draft
evalkit traces mapping list myagent
evalkit traces mapping activate myagent 2                     # make version 2 active

Repeat until the unmapped list holds nothing that matters and the counts look right, then activate the draft with evalkit traces mapping activate myagent <version>, using the version push printed, or on the agent's Mappings tab. Pushing a document identical to the draft keeps the draft's version. The version is required, so activate makes live exactly the draft you checked, even if someone pushes another one meanwhile; an older version works too, for example to roll back. Activate prints the version it activated and the one it replaced. A coding agent activates only when the developer has approved the document.

Runs record the mapping version they were converted with; a later mapping change never alters a scored run. The Runs page converts sessions on demand with the active mapping.

docs.title: MCP
docs.text: The server is also an MCP server at http://localhost:8020/mcp (streamable HTTP). An agent connected to it can read every agent's runs and trajectories, and every experiment's scores. It cannot change anything.

docs.title: Connect
docs.text:
With an evalkit login token (evalkit login stores it in ~/.evalkit/config.toml):

claude mcp add --transport http evalkit http://localhost:8020/mcp --header "Authorization: Bearer $EVALKIT_TOKEN"

Only login tokens work here: agent tokens (evalkit tokens create) and download tickets are refused.

With single sign-on configured (auth.oidc, see Single sign-on), MCP clients that speak OAuth (Claude, Cursor, Codex) connect with the URL alone: the server points them to the identity provider, and a token issued for http://localhost:8020/mcp or for evalkit's configured audience is accepted. The token's subject must be an evalkit user, so archiving someone cuts off their MCP access too. Evalkit login tokens keep working next to it.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
Tool What it returns find_agents Agents and the id (name@workspace) the run tools take find_runs An agent's runs in a time window, newest first: id, title, time, user_id, org_id, app or eval. include adds each run's metrics, turns or tool_calls (what it called, with which arguments). failed_only keeps runs with a failure; tool_error keeps runs where that tool errored. timezone reads date-only bounds as get_run_stats does. Up to 5,000 rows when listing alone, 200 with include or a filter get_runs Up to 200 runs by id: turns, failed turns, failures, duration, cost and where it came from, tokens, cost by model, tool errors by tool, opening question, final answer; include adds turns and tool_calls get_run_stats Totals over a time window, or one row per day, user, source, or tool that errored; group_by takes several at once and reads the window once get_trajectory One run's ATIF trajectory, paged by step, long text clipped get_run_files, download_run_file Files the run produced find_experiments, get_experiments, get_experiment_runs Experiments, their scorecard, and per-case scores with evaluator explanations

Every tool answers {data, meta}, with data a list of rows. Search tools page with limit and offset (meta.next_offset is the next page); tools that take ids answer one row per id in input order, with note: {"code": "not_found"} for an unknown one. Dates are start_date / end_date (YYYY-MM-DD, inclusive, or an ISO 8601 timestamp). Money is {"value", "unit": "currency", "currency": "USD"}. Errors read <code>: <detail>. Tools that read trajectories have a time budget for the whole call, listing included: a run not read in time comes back as a row with error and detail instead of metrics, counted in meta.failed by get_runs; ask for it again with get_runs. Optional fields with no value are left out of rows. When listing alone uses the budget, the call fails with harness_timeout; narrow the window. With failed_only or tool_error, find_runs reads the window again on every call, so take one page and fetch the runs not read with get_runs rather than paging on.

A turn is one user message and everything the agent did until the next one. cost_source is reported when the harness priced the run, estimated when evalkit priced it from token counts, mixed for both. A turn counts as failed when the harness marks a step in it with extra.is_error (see Harness API).

user_id and org_id are what the harness recorded. Resolve them to people and firms with your identity service.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
From nothing to a scored experiment on an evalkit server your team already runs. Each step links to its full page; Concepts explains the terms.

No server yet? Try locally runs one on your machine with a sample agent and your own LLM, and ends with how to deploy one for your team.

docs.title: 1. Pick how evalkit reaches your agent
docs.text:
Path What you build Pick it when SDK run + traces A Python script that calls your agent once per case, and an OpenTelemetry exporter to this server The default: start here. Runs start from your machine or CI Harness API An HTTP service: start a run, report its status, serve its ATIF trajectory A deployed agent the server should drive (shared agents, runs started from the UI), or you need the Workspace tab Harness API + traces The same service minus the trajectory endpoint; the trajectory comes from your spans You want the Harness API but your agent already emits OpenTelemetry spans

The Workspace tab on a run lists the files the agent wrote. evalkit reads them through the Harness API files endpoints, so only the two Harness API paths have it. See Harness API for what each endpoint enables.

docs.title: 2. Install and log in
docs.text:
evalkit needs Python 3.12 or newer.

uv tool install --reinstall "evalkit-py==0.4.0.dev72"
evalkit login --url http://localhost:8020

More in Install and Login.

docs.title: 3. Write evalkit.yaml and one case
docs.text:
At the root of the repository that holds your eval cases:

cases: eval/cases
fixtures: eval/fixtures

credentials:
  agents:
    myagent: env:MYAGENT_API_KEY # only for a Harness API agent that needs a key

The file holds no judge key. By default the evaluators that use a judge run on the evalkit server, with the LLM provider configured there. To judge with your own key instead, see Config.

Put the keys in a .env next to evalkit.yaml. Then create your agent on the server once:

# SDK path: a code-driven agent whose trajectory comes from its traces
evalkit agents create myagent --trajectory-source otel --mapping openinference.json
# Harness API path
evalkit agents create myagent --harness-url http://localhost:8080/evalkit/v1

openinference.json (or gen_ai.json) comes from the connect-traces skill: evalkit skills install copies it to .claude/skills/connect-traces/references/ (or .agents/skills/…). See Install. The skill also ships a mapping per popular framework (LangChain, CrewAI, LlamaIndex, Google ADK, Mastra, …); see Framework mappings.

Each directory under cases is a dataset. Add eval/cases/smoke/cases.yaml:

cases:
  - id: store-count
    input:
      question: "How many company-operated stores did Starbucks have at FY2021 year-end?"
    evaluators:
      output:
        answer_rubrics:
          rubrics:
            - rubric: "States 17,133 company-operated stores at FY2021 year-end."
              type: factual_retrieval

More in Config.

docs.title: 4. Run it
docs.text:
SDK path: install the SDK into your project (see Install). Mint an agent token and export it: evalkit tokens create --agent myagent, then export EVALKIT_OTEL_TOKEN=<token>. Then write eval/run.py:

from evalkit.sdk import run_experiment, tracing
from myagent import ask

tracing.register(agent="myagent")

def task(input: dict) -> str:
    return ask(input["question"])

if __name__ == "__main__":
    run_experiment(dataset="smoke", agent="myagent", task=task, dry_run=True)

dry_run=True runs one case without creating an experiment and prints what the server made of the spans. When it looks right, drop dry_run; run_experiment then returns a result whose url is the experiment page. More in SDK runs and Tracing.

Harness API path:

evalkit harness check myagent    # exercises every capability the harness declares
evalkit run smoke --agent myagent

A run executes every case it selects, whether the dataset is in your own workspace (smoke) or a shared one (smoke@dev). Review state never filters a run.

docs.title: 5. Read the results
docs.text: evalkit run prints the scorecard when it finishes. On this server, open the dataset under Datasets and pick the experiment. The experiment page has the scorecard; each run opens its trajectory, scores and, on the Harness API paths, its workspace files. If converted spans look wrong (missing messages, wrong span kinds), check one session with evalkit traces check myagent <session id> and see Mappings.

docs.title: 6. Attach a file to a case
docs.text:
Drop the file in the fixtures directory from your evalkit.yaml, register it once in fixtures.yaml at the root of your cases directory, and name it in the case. The context line is what the agent is told about the file.

cp ~/Downloads/meridian-balance-sheet.csv <fixtures>/
shasum -a 256 <fixtures>/meridian-balance-sheet.csv       # sha256 for the registry

# <cases>/fixtures.yaml
fixtures:
  - key: meridian-balance-sheet.csv
    sha256: 652d32…eece7
    context: Meridian's FY2025 balance sheet, USD thousands.

# in the case
- id: net-debt-fy2025
  fixtures: [meridian-balance-sheet.csv]
  input:
    question: Using only the attached file, what was net debt at FY2025 year-end?

A run or sync uploads any fixture whose sha256 the server doesn't hold yet, and the server keeps one copy per sha256. So you only need the files you touch, and if the bytes on disk don't match the registry the run stops and shows both hashes.

docs.title: 7. Iterate and promote
docs.text:
evalkit experiments list --dataset smoke       # experiment ids, newest first
evalkit summary <new-id> --baseline <old-id>    # compare two experiments: fixed, broken, gauge deltas
evalkit evaluate <experiment-id>        # re-score the same runs after an evaluator change; no agent calls
evalkit runs pull --experiment <experiment-id>   # download every run (trajectory, case, scores) to diagnose failures

Cases reach a shared dataset through a PR. On merge, CI syncs them into a shared workspace such as dev, where they start Unreviewed; a reviewer of that workspace approves them, and if dev is linked to prod, approval promotes them there. CI sync shows how to set up that CI job.

evalkit review request finance@dev --case-id net-debt-fy2025 --reviewer <user>
evalkit review approve finance@dev net-debt-fy2025   # reviewers only

If an admin linked dev to a promotion target (evalkit workspaces promote-to dev prod), that approval also lands the case in finance@prod, approved. prod takes cases only that way: no sync, no separate review. The case page in either workspace shows the other's version and links to it.

docs.title: SDK runs
docs.text:
run_experiment runs an experiment from your own code: it calls your task once per case and repetition, stores the runs on this server, and scores them with the judge, the remote evaluators of the agent's workspace and any Python evaluators you pass. The agent is a code-driven agent on the server (no harness URL), created once with evalkit agents create. Invoking the agent, timeouts and stopping are your code.

# eval/run.py — uv run python eval/run.py
from evalkit.sdk import run_experiment, RunResult, evaluator, tracing
from myagent import MyAgent, setup_tracing

setup_tracing()                          # your own OpenTelemetry provider and instrumentors
tracing.register(agent="myagent-sdk")   # add this server as an export destination
agent = MyAgent()

def task(input: dict, files: list) -> str:
    return agent.ask(input["question"], attachments=[f.path for f in files])

@evaluator(name="citation_check")
def citation_check(case, run) -> float:
    cited = {c["url"] for c in (run.output or {}).get("citations", [])}
    return 1.0 if cited >= set(case.config["required"]) else 0.0

if __name__ == "__main__":
    result = run_experiment(dataset="finance", agent="myagent-sdk", task=task,
                            evaluators=[citation_check], concurrency=4)
    print(result.url)

docs.title: The task
docs.text:
A sync or async callable. Parameters bind by name from this set, so their order does not matter; any other required parameter is an error before the first call, and an optional one keeps its default.

Parameter Value input the case input, verbatim, minus files files list[Fixture], the case's fixture files, downloaded before the call model the model argument of run_experiment, or None metadata a dict with the keys below

A Fixture has:

  • name: the fixture key the case names.
  • path: where the file sits on this machine.
  • context: the file's description from the fixture registry, or None. A Harness API agent gets the same text with each file; show it to your agent the same way (for example an "Attached files" block ahead of the question).

metadata holds:

  • session_id: the SDK's session id for this run, the session.id of its evalkit.run span.
  • experiment_id: the experiment, or None on a dry run.
  • case_id: the case.
  • repetition: 1 for the first repetition, 2 for the second, and so on.
  • tags: the case's tags.

model is the only way run_experiment(model=...) reaches your agent. The experiment records the requested model either way, so a task without a model parameter would silently run the agent's default; run_experiment prints a warning before the first call when that happens.

A task with exactly one parameter whose name is not in the table (def task(q)) receives the input. Return a str (the answer), a dict (the structured output) or a RunResult:

from evalkit.sdk import RunResult

RunResult(answer="…", output={"citations": []}, model="gpt-5",
          session_id="…",          # override the session the SDK polls
          trajectory={...})        # push an ATIF document instead of tracing

A task that raises records the run as failed with the exception and the experiment continues.

docs.title: An agent in another process
docs.text:
The SDK stamps session.id and the evalkit.* attributes only on spans made in this Python process. An agent behind HTTP or a job queue, or written in another language, joins the run in one of two ways. Pick one, not both.

  • Continue the trace. Inject the W3C trace context into the request and have the agent start its spans from it. Every span in a trace belongs to the session of the trace's root, the SDK's evalkit.run span, even if the agent stamps its own session.id or gen_ai.conversation.id.
from opentelemetry import propagate

def task(input: dict) -> str:
    headers: dict[str, str] = {}
    propagate.inject(headers)            # adds traceparent
    return httpx2.post(AGENT_URL, json=input, headers=headers).json()["answer"]
  • Return the agent's session. The agent puts its own session id on its root span as session.id, and the task returns it. Use this when the trace context cannot reach the agent, for example through a queue. The SDK moves its evalkit.run span into that session, so no empty session is left behind, and the trajectory is built from the agent's trace.
def task(input: dict) -> RunResult:
    job = agent_api.start(input["question"])           # your API returns the session it opened
    return RunResult(answer=job.wait(), session_id=job.session_id)

If your API cannot tell you the session id, send it one instead: pass metadata["session_id"] along with the job and have the agent use it as its session id (or wrap the job in tracing.eval_run(metadata), see Tracing). Its spans then join the SDK's session and the task returns only the answer.

def task(input: dict, metadata: dict) -> str:
    return queue.submit(input["question"], session_id=metadata["session_id"]).wait()

Either way the Runs page links the session to its experiment and case.

The agent's exporter needs its own token in EVALKIT_OTEL_TOKEN. Mint one with evalkit tokens create --agent <name>; it never expires. A login token is not accepted: it expires, and an exporter that holds it would drop every span with nothing but a line in its own log.

docs.title: Datasets and workspaces
docs.text:
• dataset="finance" runs your own workspace's copy; if finance is a directory under cases it is synced first.
  • dataset="finance@dev" or dataset="finance", workspace="dev" runs the shared cases, every review state included.
  • case_ids=[...], tags=[...], repetitions, model and resume=<experiment id> mean what the same options mean on evalkit run.
  • dry_run=True runs one case (dry_run=N runs N) without creating an experiment and prints the answer and what the server made of the session. If the server cannot read a session, that case prints a trajectory read failed line and the dry run goes on. Use it while wiring up tracing; the session shows on the Runs page with its case question and case id.

docs.title: Notebooks
docs.text:
run_experiment refuses to run inside a running event loop. In a notebook use the async form:

from evalkit.sdk import arun_experiment

result = await arun_experiment(dataset="finance", agent="myagent-sdk", task=task)

docs.title: The agent and the judge
docs.text:
agent="myagent-sdk" names an agent on the server; a bare name means your own workspace. Create it once:

evalkit agents create myagent-sdk --trajectory-source otel --mapping openinference.json \
  --max-concurrent-runs 4 --provides thinking=true

Its answer rule and exclude_spans live in its span mapping. evalkit.yaml is still required; it holds the cases, fixtures and credentials.

The judge is the server's default unless you pass one. An admin sets the default with evalkit judge-default set. With the default, or any other judge served by an LLM provider configured on the server (Judge(provider=...)), the evaluators that use a judge (answer_rubrics, presentation_judge, trajectory_rubrics) run on the evalkit server with its stored key; your machine needs no judge key:

from evalkit.sdk import Judge, run_experiment

run_experiment(dataset="finance", agent="myagent-sdk", task=task)  # the server's default judge
run_experiment(dataset="finance", agent="myagent-sdk", task=task,
               judge=Judge(provider="openai", model="gpt-5"))       # another provider on the server

To bring your own judge, pass its base URL and key. Those evaluators then run on your machine. evalkit sends the key only to your judge's base URL; it never stores it on the evalkit server or prints it:

run_experiment(dataset="finance", agent="myagent-sdk", task=task,
               judge=Judge(base_url="https://litellm.example.com", model="gpt-5",
                           api_key=os.environ["LITELLM_API_KEY"]))

Re-scoring such an experiment needs the key again: pass the same judge, key included, to evaluate_experiment(experiment_id=..., judge=Judge(...)). A different judge (another endpoint or model, or other settings) is refused.

A judge sets provider or base_url, never both. tool_trajectory_match, required_tools_called and max_response_time always run on your machine. The run page shows server or local beside each score.

docs.title: Capabilities
docs.text:
A code-driven agent has no GET /capabilities, so evalkit writes its capabilities onto each experiment itself: trajectory, tool_calls, token_usage and run_listing are true; thinking, artifacts and workspace are false. Evaluators gated on a capability skip when it is false. evalkit does not read capabilities from the spans. Set provides on the agent (evalkit agents create --provides, or evalkit agents edit) to declare what it really does, for example thinking: true when its spans carry the model's reasoning. Declare only what works: a false true produces failing scores blamed on the agent.

The agent's input schema is the default (a required string question) unless you set one with evalkit agents create --input-schema or evalkit agents edit --input-schema. Every case input must pass it, in a dry run too; see Input schema.

docs.title: Python evaluators
docs.text: @evaluator(name=..., kind="evaluator" | "gauge", requires_trajectory=False) turns a function into an evaluator. It receives the same EvalCase and EvalRun the HTTP Custom Evaluator API sends: the case id, input, expected block and this evaluator's config from the case YAML; the answer, structured output and the ATIF trajectory as a dict. Return a float, a ScoreItem (from evalkit.sdk import ScoreItem), or a list of them. Case schema lists the fields of EvalCase and EvalRun. A case selects it by name under evaluators.custom, exactly like an HTTP evaluator.

docs.title: Bring your own benchmark
docs.text:
A published benchmark is a suite plus a Python evaluator:

  1. Write a script that turns the benchmark's file into case YAML. Each case gets the question as input. Its grading data (rubrics, reference answer) goes under evaluators.custom.<grader name>.
  2. evalkit sync <dir> puts it in a dataset like any suite.
  3. Write the grader as an @evaluator with that name. It reads the grading data from case.config, and calls its own judge models if it needs any. Pass it to run_experiment.

evalkit lint and evalkit sync warn with W-CUSTOM-UNKNOWN for the grader name, because the server can't see a Python evaluator. That warning is expected.

docs.title: Re-scoring
docs.text:
Python evaluators live in your script, so a re-score that needs them starts from the script:

from evalkit.sdk import evaluate_experiment

evaluate_experiment(experiment_id="…", evaluators=[citation_check],
                    refetch_trajectories=True)

refetch_trajectories polls the collector again for runs whose trajectory was partial or unavailable and re-scores them. evalkit evaluate refuses experiments that used Python evaluators and points here.

Next: Tracing.

docs.title: Server config: config.yaml
docs.text:
config.yaml configures one evalkit server. evalkit serve and evalkit db upgrade read it (--config, default ./config.yaml) and load the .env beside it; the environment wins. It is not evalkit.yaml, the developer config (Config).

Any value can be env:NAME (required) or env:NAME:<default>. Unknown keys fail the start.

evalkit init-server writes one for a single machine, with a smaller database pool than the defaults below.

docs.title: Database pool and scoring
docs.text:
Key Default init-server What it does db.pool_size 20 5 Connections one server keeps open to Postgres. db.max_overflow 10 5 Extra connections opened under load. db.pool_timeout_seconds 5 5 A request that waits this long for a connection gets 503 with Retry-After. runner.evaluation_concurrency 16 4 Runs a server run scores at once; also the most a run may ask for.
  • One server holds at most pool_size + max_overflow connections.
  • Keep (pool_size + max_overflow) × servers well under Postgres max_connections (100 on a stock Postgres), with room for migrations and psql. Ten servers at the defaults need 300 and fail with FATAL: sorry, too many clients already.
  • Keep evaluation_concurrency under pool_size: each run being scored holds a connection while it saves.
  • The CLI and the SDK retry a 503. A server run does not; if one fails for lack of a connection, evalkit evaluate <experiment> finishes it.

docs.title: Every key
docs.text:
Key Default What it does server.base_url required The URL in links the CLI prints. evalkit serve binds its port (8020 when it has none) unless --port is given. server.accent_color none A CSS color for a strip along the top of every web UI page, so each environment is told apart at a glance. db.url required Postgres URL, e.g. postgresql+psycopg://localhost/evalkit. db.migrate_on_start false Run evalkit db upgrade at startup. db.pool_size, db.max_overflow, db.pool_timeout_seconds 20, 10, 5 See Database pool and scoring. blob.url required Where trajectories, artifacts and fixtures go: file:///path or s3://bucket/prefix. runner.evaluation_concurrency 16 See Database pool and scoring. cost_map.source bundled The LiteLLM cost map: bundled, or a path or URL. auth.token_ttl_hours 720 How long a login token lasts. mcp.oauth none Also accept an OAuth provider's JWTs at /mcp: issuer, jwks_uri, audience (none), algorithm (RS256), scope (evalkit:read). See MCP. otel.settle_seconds 10 A session is settled when its newest span arrived longer ago than this. otel.max_batch_bytes 16777216 (16 MB) One OTLP export request; 413 beyond it. otel.max_session_bytes 402653184 (384 MB) Span attributes one session read loads; 413 beyond it. Size it with the server's memory. otel.import_page_traces 25 Traces per request to a trace source during an import. limits.fixture_upload_bytes 524288000 (500 MB) One fixture file uploaded by evalkit sync. limits.experiment_blob_bytes 524288000 (500 MB) One trajectory or artifact written by a local run. limits.case_upload_bytes 52428800 (50 MB) The case YAML of one evalkit sync or lint. limits.request_bytes 10485760 (10 MB) Any other request body. sentry none Report server errors to Sentry: dsn (required), environment, traces_sample_rate (0.0), max_request_body_size (never, small, medium or always). encryption_key none Fernet key that encrypts stored API keys. The server refuses to start without it once any exist. allow_private_endpoints false Let agents, evaluators, LLM providers and trace sources point at loopback, private or link-local addresses.

LLM providers, the default judge and stored API keys live in the database, not here: set them with evalkit llm-providers, evalkit judge-default set and evalkit agents edit.

docs.title: Single sign-on
docs.text: Evalkit signs people in through your identity provider (IdP) with OpenID Connect. The web UI and the CLI are public OAuth clients: each sends you to the IdP, receives an access token, and sends that token to evalkit with every request. Evalkit verifies it with the IdP's published keys and never issues a login token of its own for SSO users. CI pipelines use a machine client at the IdP. This page is for the IdP admin who registers evalkit and the evalkit admin who turns SSO on.

docs.title: What evalkit is to the IdP
docs.text: Piece At the IdP Standard The web UI and the CLI One public client (no secret) Authorization code with PKCE, RFC 6749 §4.1 and RFC 7636; refresh, RFC 6749 §6 The CLI on a machine without a browser The same client Device authorization grant, RFC 8628 Evalkit's API An API or resource that access tokens name in aud JWT access tokens, RFC 9068 A CI pipeline One machine client per pipeline, with a secret Client credentials, RFC 6749 §4.4 Discovery <issuer>/.well-known/openid-configuration OpenID Connect Discovery 1.0

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Check each before registering. Evalkit does not work around any of them.

Requirement How to check OIDC discovery at the issuer curl <issuer>/.well-known/openid-configuration returns jwks_uri, authorization_endpoint, token_endpoint JWT access tokens, not opaque strings, that carry evalkit's audience in aud Decode an access token issued for evalkit (jwt.io or evalkit whoami after a sign-in); it has three dot-separated parts and aud contains the value you configure as auth.oidc.audience. Google and Okta's default authorization server issue opaque tokens and cannot be used; Okta needs a custom authorization server sub, exp, iat in every access token Same decoded token email and, when the IdP has one, preferred_username in the ID token Grant the email and profile scopes to the client; evalkit refuses a first sign-in whose ID token has no email PKCE with S256 for the public client A setting on the client registration Refresh tokens for the public client, with rotation on Required, not recommended: the web UI keeps its refresh token in browser storage and rotation is what bounds the damage of a stolen one The client credentials grant for machine clients A setting on each machine client The device authorization grant, optional Needed only for evalkit login --no-browser CORS on the discovery document and the token endpoint for evalkit's origin The web UI calls both from the browser. curl -i -H 'Origin: https://<evalkit>' <token_endpoint> answers with Access-Control-Allow-Origin

docs.title: Registering the public client
docs.text:
One registration, shared by the UI and the CLI. Application type: public, single-page or native, no client secret. Redirect URIs:

  • https://<evalkit>/login/callback for the web UI.
  • http://127.0.0.1/callback for the CLI, with any port (RFC 8252 §7.3; Okta and Entra accept the loopback with a wildcard port, Keycloak accepts http://127.0.0.1:*/callback).

Scopes to allow: openid, profile, email, offline_access (or the IdP's name for refresh tokens). PKCE S256 on. Refresh token rotation on. Copy the client id into auth.oidc.client_id.

docs.title: Registering the audience
docs.text:
Access tokens must name evalkit. How that is set up depends on the IdP:

IdP How What goes in config Entra ID Expose an API on the app registration with a scope such as api://<app id>/evalkit; grant the public client that scope audience: api://<app id>; add the scope to scopes Okta (custom authorization server) Set the server's audience to evalkit's URL audience: https://evalkit.example.com; authorize_params: {resource: https://evalkit.example.com} if the server needs a resource indicator Auth0 Create an API with evalkit's URL as identifier audience: https://evalkit.example.com; authorize_params: {audience: https://evalkit.example.com} Keycloak Add an audience mapper for the client audience: <the mapped value> Any IdP that follows RFC 8707 Resource indicators authorize_params: {resource: <audience>}

Evalkit sends authorize_params verbatim on the authorize request and the device authorization request; the server never interprets them.

docs.title: Registering a machine client for CI
docs.text: One per pipeline. Application type: machine-to-machine or service, client credentials grant on, with the same audience attached. Note the client id and secret: they go into the pipeline's secrets as EVALKIT_OIDC_CLIENT_ID and EVALKIT_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET. Note the subject the IdP puts in sub for this client's tokens (Okta and Auth0 derive it from the client id; Entra uses the service principal's object id; Keycloak the id of the client's service account user): an evalkit admin binds it with evalkit users add ci-bot --subject <sub>. See CI sync.

docs.title: The evalkit side
docs.text:
In the server's config.yaml:

auth:
  token_ttl_hours: 720          # password login tokens
  password_login: admin         # admin (default) or all; ignored without oidc
  oidc:
    issuer: https://id.example.com
    client_id: 0oa1b2c3d4e5f6g7h8
    audience: https://evalkit.example.com
    name: Okta                  # the login button's label
    scopes: [openid, profile, email, offline_access]
    required_scopes: []         # scopes an access token must carry
    authorize_params: {}
    algorithms: [RS256]
    admin_claim: null           # {name: roles, value: evalkit-admin}: who is an admin

password_login: admin keeps password login for admins only, so the bootstrap admin account stays a break-glass login while everyone else uses SSO. all runs both side by side. Restart the server and check GET /api/auth/providers: it lists the IdP's name and endpoints, or answers 503 while the IdP is unreachable (the server still starts, and admin password login keeps working).

docs.title: Requiring a scope
docs.text:
Some IdPs issue evalkit-audience tokens to anyone with an account. Set auth.oidc.required_scopes to a scope that only authorised people get, and evalkit refuses every other IdP token:

auth:
  oidc:
    scopes: [openid, profile, email, offline_access, evalkit:read]
    required_scopes: [evalkit:read]

The server refuses to start when a required scope is not also in scopes: the UI, the CLI and MCP hosts only request the scopes listed there.

  • The check covers POST /api/auth/oidc/register (no user is created), every /api request with an IdP token, and /mcp.
  • evalkit reads the scopes from the access token's scope claim (a space-separated string), its scp claim (a list, or a space-separated string), or both.
  • A token that lacks one answers 403 access token lacks required scope <scope> on /api and on register. This check runs before evalkit looks for the user, so a token without the scope gets 403 even for an unregistered identity. /mcp answers 403 insufficient_scope ("Required scope: ") with a WWW-Authenticate header.
  • Put each required scope in auth.oidc.scopes too, so the UI and the CLI ask the IdP for it.
  • The CLI's CI login (client credentials) asks the IdP for the required scopes, which GET /api/auth/providers lists as required_scopes. Let the CI machine client request them at the IdP. It does not ask for the rest of scopes, because IdPs such as Okta refuse openid and offline_access there.
  • Password login tokens and agent tokens are not checked. An empty list (the default) turns the check off.

docs.title: Several organisations
docs.text:
Everyone who signs in lands in one tenant. A deployment that serves several organisations from one server runs evalkit inside a wrapper that owns its tenants: it passes create_app(resolve_tenant=...), which reads the organisation from the access token and returns its id, which evalkit stores on every row as text (1-64 letters, digits, - or _; anything else answers 403). A server without a wrapper puts everything in default. evalkit keeps no list of tenants itself.

The wrapper resolves every token the same way, CI's client credentials tokens included, so the IdP must put the organisation in those too. When the wrapper returns no tenant, the request answers 403 no tenant for this request; /mcp can only accept or refuse a token, so there it answers 401.

docs.title: Admins from the IdP
docs.text:
auth:
  oidc:
    admin_claim:
      name: roles               # the access token claim
      value: evalkit-admin      # the value that makes an admin

With admin_claim set, every registration (each sign-in) sets the person's admin flag from the access token: admin when the claim equals the value, or is a list that contains it; not an admin otherwise. A person the IdP stops naming as an admin loses admin at their next sign-in, even when they are the tenant's last admin: the IdP owns admins once this is on, so evalkit users demote's last-admin check does not apply. Unset (the default), registration never changes the flag, and admins are promoted with evalkit users promote. An admin's powers stay inside their tenant: users, workspaces and members, LLM providers and the default judge, trace sources and agent tokens of that tenant only.

mcp.oauth is gone: /mcp verifies tokens with the same settings as /api, and an IdP token is an evalkit user there too.

docs.title: Signing in to the web UI
docs.text: In the web UI, the login page shows Continue with when single sign-on is configured.
