The first sign-in creates your evalkit user from the identity provider's account; later sign-ins find it. An admin can still use the username and password form behind Admin sign-in (or under the button when auth.password_login is all). The profile button at the bottom of the sidebar shows your email under your username. Sign out clears the session in this browser only; your identity provider session stays.

docs.title: Admin runbook
docs.text:
1. Start with EVALKIT_ADMIN_PASSWORD set, as before; admin is a password account.
  2. Ask the first person to sign in; evalkit creates their user on the first sign-in. Then evalkit users promote <username>.
  3. Bind machine users: evalkit users add ci-bot --subject <sub>, then evalkit workspaces members add dev ci-bot --role writer.
  4. A sign-in that answers 409 username <x> is taken by a user or workspace means the derived username (the part before @ in preferred_username, else in email) already exists. Link the identity to the account you choose: evalkit users bind <username> --subject <sub> (the 409 names the subject). A password account that predates SSO is linked the same way.
  5. Revoke: evalkit users archive <username> blocks the next request. The IdP's own revocation takes effect within one access token lifetime.

docs.title: Tracing
docs.text:
The collector is an OTLP/HTTP endpoint on this server:

POST http://localhost:8020/api/otel/v1/traces

It accepts application/x-protobuf and application/json, gzip or not, from any OpenTelemetry SDK. Spans are stored as received and converted to ATIF with the agent's mapping when a run or the Runs page asks for them.

docs.title: From Python with the SDK
docs.text:
from evalkit.sdk import tracing

tracing.register(agent="myagent-sdk")

register adds an exporter for this server to your global tracer provider, creating one if none is set. Your existing exporters keep running. The exporter carries an X-Evalkit-Agent header, which names the agent on the server; the evalkit.agent resource attribute is only set when register creates the provider itself. It reads the server URL from EVALKIT_SERVER_URL or your evalkit login, and the token from EVALKIT_OTEL_TOKEN, an agent token (evalkit tokens create --agent <agent>); a login token is not accepted, because it expires under a long-running process. It needs the otel extra.

docs.title: An existing span pipeline
docs.text:
register changes the global provider. When you build your own pipeline, take evalkit's parts and put them where you need them:

from evalkit.sdk import tracing

exporter = tracing.exporter(agent="myagent-sdk")    # OTLPSpanExporter: URL, token and X-Evalkit-Agent set
processor = tracing.processor(agent="myagent-sdk")  # batch processor around that exporter
provider.add_span_processor(processor)              # what register does for you
headers = tracing.headers(agent="myagent-sdk")      # the same headers, for an exporter you build yourself

All three resolve the server and token the same way register does. processor also stamps the run's session.id and evalkit.* attributes on spans that start under a task call (or under tracing.eval_run, below).

Spans handed straight to a processor or exporter, for example by a bridge that converts another tool's spans, never pass through the provider, so register cannot see them. Hand them to tracing.processor(...) too: give the bridge that processor, or one processor that fans out to all of yours and evalkit's (OpenTelemetry's SynchronousMultiSpanProcessor). Those spans are already finished, so processor cannot stamp them: the bridge copies session.id onto each span it converts. How eval-only export treats them is below.

docs.title: Choosing what a shared worker exports
docs.text:
A worker that serves both app runs (production, staging or manual use) and eval runs exports every span it makes, so every app turn also becomes a session on this server, which you can browse on the Runs page and pull with evalkit runs pull <agent> --source app. Whether to send app traffic is your choice. eval_run marks eval runs either way, and to send only those, filter on the mark:

from evalkit.sdk import tracing

provider.add_span_processor(tracing.processor(agent="myagent", only=tracing.is_eval_span))

def handle_job(job):
    if job.evalkit:                           # the task's metadata, sent along with the job
        with tracing.eval_run(job.evalkit):
            return run_agent(job)
    return run_agent(job)

The task passes its metadata argument along with the job (see SDK runs). eval_run stamps session.id (the SDK's session id), evalkit.case_id, evalkit.experiment_id and evalkit.repetition on every span started inside it, so the worker's spans join the run's session and the task returns only the answer. is_eval_span is true for a span that carries evalkit.case_id. The stamp lives in a context variable: spans started in another thread need that thread to run inside eval_run too.

A harness agent learns that a run is an eval run from the metadata of POST /runs: experiment_id, case_id and repetition. That is what it passes to eval_run, with the run_id it returns as the session id: tracing.eval_run({**metadata, "session_id": run_id}).

only decides by trace, not by span. It is any function that takes a span and returns a bool, and it runs on each span as the span starts and again as it ends. Once it is true for one span, the processor keeps every span of that span's trace that reaches it: spans started inside eval_run, the job's own spans started before eval_run in the same trace, and finished spans a bridge hands straight to the processor. Spans of other traces are dropped. A custom only picks whole traces the same way.

The rule for order: a span is kept when its trace is already marked by the time the span ends. The first span started inside eval_run marks its trace as it starts, before anything under it ends, so spans that end before it and spans a bridge hands over later are both kept. A span that ends before any span of its trace was marked is dropped. A bridge that may hand spans over that early can copy the evalkit.* attributes onto them, so each one marks its own trace. A bridge should copy session.id either way: the server gives each span the session of its outermost ancestor that carries one, and the span's own session.id when no ancestor does.

The processor remembers the 10,000 most recently used eval traces and forgets the oldest. Each kept span refreshes its trace, so a trace is only forgotten once 10,000 other eval traces have been used since its last span.

Spans from another process in the same trace, such as an MCP gateway pod the agent calls, never reach this processor. They go through that process's own exporter, so that process makes its own choice: either it continues the trace, wraps its work in eval_run with the run's metadata sent along with the request, and filters with only=tracing.is_eval_span too, or it exports everything.

Do not use a sampler for this: a sampler drops spans for every exporter, your own backend included.

Around every task call the SDK opens a root span named evalkit.run with session.id set to the run id, and stamps session.id, evalkit.experiment_id, evalkit.case_id and evalkit.repetition onto every span your code starts underneath it. That is what groups a trace into one session. When the task returns RunResult(session_id=...), the root span takes that session id instead, so it joins the agent's session rather than sitting alone; see SDK runs for agents in another process.

docs.title: From any OpenTelemetry SDK
docs.text:
Point the exporter at the collector and name the agent, either with a header or an attribute:

export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_ENDPOINT=http://localhost:8020/api/otel/v1/traces
export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS="Authorization=Bearer <token>,X-Evalkit-Agent=myagent"
export OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES="evalkit.agent=myagent"   # alternative to the header

The collector picks the agent per span: the span's evalkit.agent attribute first, then the resource's, then the X-Evalkit-Agent header. One process that serves several agents can therefore share one exporter and set evalkit.agent on each agent's spans. The value is an agent reference (myagent or myagent@workspace). Every agent a batch names is checked as if it came in the header: an agent token writes only its own agent, a login token only agents in workspaces you can write to (your own, or a shared one where you are a writer). If any span names an agent the token may not write, the whole batch is refused.

Put the session id on the outermost span of each turn, in the attribute your mapping's session_id rule names (session.id in openinference.json, gen_ai.conversation.id in gen_ai.json). Each span belongs to the session of its outermost ancestor that carries one, even when the span carries a session attribute of its own. A span with no such ancestor keeps its own session. So a root span with a session sets the session for the whole trace, and a root span without one (an HTTP server's request span) does not matter.

docs.title: Agent behind an HTTP server
docs.text:
When the agent runs behind FastAPI, Express or any other instrumented HTTP server, the server's request span (POST /chat) is the root of the trace and carries no session id. Pick one:

  • Start a span of your own around each turn and put the session id on it. The agent's spans underneath join that session:
with tracer.start_as_current_span("turn", attributes={"session.id": session_id}):
    answer = await agent.run(question)
  • With OpenInference, wrap the turn in using_session(session_id); it stamps session.id onto every span started inside it:
from openinference.instrumentation import using_session

with using_session(session_id):
    answer = await agent.run(question)
  • Turn off the server framework's tracing, so the agent's own spans are the roots.

Pydantic AI sets its own gen_ai.conversation.id on its spans. Your turn span's id already wins over it in evalkit. Passing yours anyway, agent.run(question, conversation_id=session_id), is optional: it keeps the ids the same in other trace tools.

evalkit traces check warns when a session's trace root is outside the session and names the top span the session starts from.

docs.title: Deployed agents
docs.text:
A service cannot carry a person's token. Mint an agent token, bound to one agent and valid only for the collector:

evalkit tokens create --agent ouragent@dev     # needs writer on dev
evalkit tokens list
evalkit tokens revoke <id>

Set it on the deployment as EVALKIT_OTEL_TOKEN next to EVALKIT_SERVER_URL; tracing.register, tracing.exporter and tracing.processor require the token. For a non-Python exporter put it in OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS. Use an agent token for any exporter outside the process that calls run_experiment too, even on your laptop: the login token expires under a long-running worker.

The collector logs every refused export as otel export rejected with the status, the reason (expired token, invalid token, unknown agent, forbidden, too large, malformed) and the agent. OpenTelemetry exporters only log a failed export on their side, so a silent agent is worth checking in both logs.

docs.title: Size limits and large spans
docs.text:
LLM spans from OpenInference and GenAI instrumentations carry the full input of each call: the messages so far, the system prompt and the tool schemas. Every turn repeats the whole context, so a long agent session grows with roughly the square of its turns. A 14-minute chat with subagents can store hundreds of MB of span attributes.

The server has two limits, both set in its config:

Limit Default What happens past it otel.max_batch_bytes 16 MiB One export request (after gzip is undone) gets 413 and its spans are dropped. Exporters do not split a refused batch, so keep batches small. otel.max_session_bytes 384 MiB Reading the session (a run's trajectory, evalkit traces check, the Mappings tab) gets 413 with the session's size and the limit. A run records the trajectory as unavailable and logs the message. --dump spans.json still works.

otel.max_session_bytes counts the span attributes a trajectory build loads, not everything stored. evalkit reads the input messages (and system prompt) of an LLM span only for the first LLM call under each root span and in each subagent; later calls add only their output, tool calls and tokens to the trajectory. So the build leaves the input of every later LLM call in the database and does not count it. The limit keeps one session from using up the server's memory, so raise it only together with the server's memory limit.

For agents with large spans, send fewer spans per export and give each export more time. For the Python SDK, tracing.register included:

export OTEL_BSP_MAX_EXPORT_BATCH_SIZE=16   # spans per export; default 512
export OTEL_BSP_MAX_QUEUE_SIZE=2048        # spans waiting for export; raise it if the exporter logs "Queue full"
export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TIMEOUT=60       # seconds per export in Python; default 10

OpenTelemetry SDKs keep at most 128 attributes per span (OTEL_SPAN_ATTRIBUTE_COUNT_LIMIT). OpenInference writes each message as several attributes (llm.input_messages.0.message.role, ….content, …), so a long conversation passes the limit and the SDK drops attributes, which loses messages or parts of them. The Python SDK logs "Attributes dict is full" when it happens. Each exported span says how many attributes it lost; evalkit stores that count, and evalkit traces check warns on its llm line when an LLM span lost any. Raise the limit before the SDK starts:

export OTEL_SPAN_ATTRIBUTE_COUNT_LIMIT=4096

Other SDKs follow the OpenTelemetry spec and read OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TIMEOUT in milliseconds (60000). A 10 MB span can take more than 10 s to upload, longer than the default timeout. In an OpenTelemetry Collector, set send_batch_max_size on the batch processor and timeout on the otlphttp exporter instead.

docs.title: Exporting to evalkit and another backend
docs.text:
The standard OTLP variables name one endpoint. To keep exporting to your tracing backend and send the same spans here, either:

  • add a second otlphttp exporter to the OpenTelemetry Collector the agent already exports to (recommended for deployed agents), or
  • add a second span processor and exporter in code. tracing.register does this for Python.
exporters:
  otlphttp/evalkit:
    traces_endpoint: http://localhost:8020/api/otel/v1/traces
    headers:
      Authorization: Bearer ${env:EVALKIT_OTEL_TOKEN}
      X-Evalkit-Agent: ouragent@dev
service:
  pipelines:
    traces:
      exporters: [otlp/existing, otlphttp/evalkit]

The collector speaks OTLP over HTTP only, not gRPC. Bodies may be chunked with no Content-Length (the JavaScript exporter sends them that way); a proxy in front of the collector must allow that.

docs.title: The main agent and subagents
docs.text:
An AGENT span (openinference.span.kind=AGENT, or gen_ai.operation.name=invoke_agent) becomes a subagent trajectory only when another agent started it: it sits under a tool span, or it carries the tool_call_id of the call that started it. The subagent is named by the span's agent.name (gen_ai.agent.name), or by the span name when that is missing. Every other AGENT span is part of the main agent's own work, so an outer wrapper span, graph nodes tagged AGENT and one root span per chat turn all end up in one trajectory.

The main agent is the root span when it is an AGENT span; otherwise, as with the SDK's evalkit.run span, the earliest AGENT span that is not inside another one. When a session holds several root spans, one per chat turn, evalkit puts them in time order and takes the answer from the last one.

Each user message appears in the trajectory once, as a user step, before the first LLM call that has it in its input. So a chat's later turns show up as new user steps. Two limits:

  • evalkit loads the input messages only of the first LLM call under each root span (see the size limit above). When every turn of a chat runs inside one trace, only the first user message is loaded; give each turn its own root span to see them all.
  • When a framework sends only the latest user message instead of the whole history, evalkit adds a user step for each text it has not seen yet. A user message repeated word for word ("yes", then "yes" again) then shows up once.

Two mapping fields change this when the shape is wrong for your agent: main_agent pins the main agent, and subagent_spans keeps sibling agents (a crew whose agents hand over without a tool call) as separate subagent trajectories. See Mappings.

docs.title: Harness agents with traces
docs.text:
A harness agent created with --trajectory-source otel keeps the whole Harness API flow and skips GET /runs/{id}/trajectory: it puts the run id it returned on its spans, in the attribute its mapping's session_id rule names, and evalkit polls the session until it settles. The harness declares provides.trajectory: false; evalkit still runs the trajectory evaluators because the trajectory comes from the collector.

The session evalkit polls is the run_id that POST /runs returns, so there is no separate session field. A queue-backed agent whose worker picks its own session id returns that id as run_id, or puts the run_id it returned on its spans in that session attribute. To export only eval runs from a harness that also serves production, see Choosing what a shared worker exports above.

docs.title: Importing history from a trace source
docs.text:
An admin registers a trace source (a Phoenix server) once. After that, any user can import traces from it into an OTel agent they can write, with evalkit traces import or the agent page's Import tab.

  • The trace source's API key is shared with every user in effect: anyone can import any project that key can read.
  • Imported traces land in the agent's workspace. Every user can read every workspace, so traces imported into your personal workspace are visible to everyone on the server. See Where runs happen.

docs.title: Message roles
docs.text:
evalkit reads message roles in any letter case and maps the names some frameworks use to four roles:

Role on the span Read as assistant, model (Gemini, Google ADK), ai (LangChain), bot assistant user, human user system, developer (OpenAI) system tool, function tool

The trajectory drops messages with any other role, along with their tool calls. evalkit traces check warns on its llm line and names the unknown roles it found.

docs.title: Checking a session
docs.text:
evalkit traces check myagent-sdk <session id>

prints the settle state, span kinds, tokens, the attributes the mapping did not read and the ATIF summary. --dump spans.json writes the raw spans. --dump esf.json leaves out the input messages of every LLM call after each agent's first, as the trajectory does not use them; spans.json has the raw values. A session over otel.max_session_bytes fails the check with its size and the limit (see Size limits and large spans above). If the kinds or messages look wrong, the agent needs a mapping: see Mappings, and Framework mappings for a ready-made one per framework.

docs.title: Try evalkit locally
docs.text:
The try-it stack runs evalkit on your machine and walks you through the default way to connect an agent: an SDK run with OpenTelemetry traces. Your Python code calls the agent once per case. The agent's spans go to evalkit, evalkit turns them into a trajectory, and your LLM judges the answers. The kit includes a small sample agent that calls your LLM, so you get a real scorecard before you touch your own agent.

It is not a deployment: it uses a demo admin password and keeps everything on one machine. For a real deployment, follow the evalkit-deployment skill.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• uv.
  • An OpenAI-compatible LLM endpoint (OpenAI, a LiteLLM proxy, vLLM, Ollama, ...) that supports tool calls and structured output, with its base URL, API key and model name. The sample agent and the judge both use it.
  • Either Postgres 15 or newer running on this machine (without Docker), or Docker with Compose v2 (with Docker).

docs.title: Start the server
docs.text:
Pick one way. Both end with the server on the port you picked (8020 by default) and the try kit in a folder, and the steps after this section are the same.

To use another port, run evalkit init-server --port 9500 without Docker (evalkit serve reads it from config.yaml), or set EVALKIT_PORT=9500 in .env with Docker.

docs.title: Without Docker
docs.text:
evalkit is on PyPI as evalkit-py and needs Python 3.12 or newer. Install it with the server extra, then let evalkit init-server set up the rest:

uv tool install --reinstall "evalkit-py[server]==0.4.0.dev72"   # or: pip install "evalkit-py[server]==0.4.0.dev72"
evalkit init-server
cd evalkit-try
evalkit serve

init-server asks for the Postgres URL (default postgresql+psycopg://localhost/evalkit), your LLM's base URL, model and API key, and the admin password (default evalkit-admin). A question is skipped when its flag or environment variable is set (evalkit init-server --help lists both); --yes never asks. It then:

  • creates the database when it does not exist, and migrates it
  • registers your LLM as the LLM provider test-llm and makes it the default judge, with its API key stored encrypted in the database
  • copies the try kit into ./evalkit-try
  • writes config.yaml there, with blobs stored under evalkit-try/data and a database pool sized for one machine (Server config lists every key and its default)
  • writes .env beside it, with your LLM settings, the admin password and the key that encrypts stored API keys; evalkit serve reads it. Keep .env: without that key the server cannot read the stored LLM key

Leave evalkit serve running and use another terminal for the steps below, from the evalkit-try folder. The CLI is already installed, so skip the install command in step 1.

docs.title: With Docker
docs.text:
The kit is skills/evalkit-deployment/try/ in the evalkit repository, and the server image holds a copy. The first --build takes a few minutes (it builds the web UI and installs the server); later starts take seconds.

From an evalkit checkout, compose builds the image:

cd skills/evalkit-deployment/try
cp -n .env.example .env          # fill in LLM_BASE_URL, LLM_API_KEY, LLM_MODEL
docker compose up -d --wait --build

With the server image instead, copy the kit out of it first:

export EVALKIT_IMAGE=<registry>/evalkit:<tag>
docker run --rm --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -v "$PWD:/out" "$EVALKIT_IMAGE" \
  evalkit init-server --kit-only --dir /out/evalkit-try
cd evalkit-try
cp -n .env.example .env          # fill in LLM_BASE_URL, LLM_API_KEY, LLM_MODEL
docker compose up -d --wait

Compose starts Postgres and the evalkit server, with your LLM as the judge. --wait returns once the server is healthy. The server runs migrations on every start.

docs.title: What's in the kit
docs.text: File What it is agent.py The sample agent. It answers questions about Acme Widgets, a made-up company, by calling your LLM with one tool, lookup_financials. It records each model call and tool call as an OpenTelemetry span, using the GenAI semantic conventions. run.py The SDK run: tracing.register sends the spans to evalkit, and run_experiment calls the agent once per case and scores the answers. mapping.json The span mapping: which span attribute holds the model, the messages, the tokens and each tool call. It starts as the connect-traces skill's gen_ai.json. cases/acme/ Five cases in two folders (tags), with answer rubrics and a tool check. evalkit.yaml, .env Where the cases are. config.yaml The server's config. docker-compose.yml, .env.example With Docker only: the stack, and the template for its .env. init-server leaves them out.

docs.title: 1. Install the CLI and log in
docs.text:
uv tool install --reinstall "evalkit-py==0.4.0.dev72"   # with Docker only
evalkit login --url http://localhost:8020 --username admin --password evalkit-admin

0.4.0.dev72 is the server's version; curl http://localhost:8020/api/cli prints it.

evalkit login replaces any login you already saved. To keep it, skip evalkit login and give this shell a token for the try-it server instead (this needs jq):

export EVALKIT_SERVER_URL=http://localhost:8020
export EVALKIT_TOKEN=$(curl -fsSL -X POST http://localhost:8020/api/auth/login \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"username": "admin", "password": "evalkit-admin"}' | jq -r .token)

run.py declares its own dependencies at the top of the file, so uv run run.py installs what it needs on the first run. The kit pins evalkit to the server's version when evalkit init-server copies it. In an evalkit checkout, run the kit's scripts with the checkout instead: uv run --project ../../.. --extra otel python run.py.

docs.title: 2. Connect the agent's traces
docs.text:
Create the agent. Its trajectories come from its spans, read with mapping.json:

evalkit agents create analyst --trajectory-source otel --mapping mapping.json

Run one case without creating an experiment:

uv run run.py --dry-run

It prints the answer, the session id with a count of its spans by kind and the mapping version, and whether evalkit built a valid trajectory from them. If no spans arrived, check that run.py calls tracing.register before the agent runs.

Then see how the mapping read that session:

evalkit traces check analyst <session id>

It prints one line per check: the session settled, the root span, the mapping version, the model calls and their token totals, the tool calls matched to the model's calls, any span attribute the mapping does not read, and a summary of the trajectory. Every line should have a ✓.

docs.title: 3. First scorecard
docs.text:
uv run run.py

run_experiment syncs cases/acme into your own workspace (acme@admin), runs the five cases, has your LLM judge each answer against its rubrics, checks that the agent called lookup_financials, and prints the scorecard and the experiment URL. The scores depend on your model. acme-operating-margin asks for a figure the agent has no data for, so it passes only if the agent says so instead of making one up.

The answer_rubric_* rows by rubric type (factual_retrieval, derived_computation, analysis_interpretation) count only the cases that have a rubric of that type, so their case counts differ.

Open http://localhost:8020, log in as admin with the admin password, and open the experiment under the acme dataset. Each run shows its trajectory, the judge's verdict on every rubric and the tool check. The Runs page lists the raw sessions.

docs.title: 4. Iterate
docs.text:
This is the loop you will run on your own agent:

  • Change the agent, for example the instructions in agent.py, and run run.py again. Compare the two experiments in the UI.
  • Edit or add a case under cases/acme/ and run again. The run syncs the folder first.
  • Run one folder: run_experiment(..., tags=["balance-sheet"]). A folder's name is a tag on its cases.

docs.title: 5. Connect your own agent
docs.text:
Do the same in your own repository:

  1. Traces. If your agent already emits OpenTelemetry spans (OpenInference or GenAI conventions), keep them. If not, add an instrumentor for your LLM library, for example openinference-instrumentation-openai for the OpenAI client (OpenInference publishes one per popular library), or record GenAI spans yourself as this kit's agent.py does (Tracing). The connect-traces skill writes or checks the span mapping (Mappings).
  2. Setup. Put an evalkit.yaml at the root of your repository, with cases: pointing at your cases directory. Keep any keys it names in a .env beside it.
  3. Judge. Nothing to set up: the evaluators that use a judge run on the evalkit server, with the LLM provider configured there as the default judge. To judge with your own key instead, see Config.
  4. Script. Copy run.py. Pin evalkit in its header to your evalkit server's version (evalkit-py[otel]==<version>), call tracing.register(agent="myagent"), and write a task that calls your agent with the case input. uv run run.py builds an environment from the header alone, so add your agent's packages to its dependencies. If your agent lives in a uv project, you can instead add evalkit to the project (see the Install page) and run the script with uv run python run.py.
  5. Cases. Add a folder under your cases directory, for example mine/, and run with dataset="mine". The authoring-eval-cases skill covers the format. See Concepts for the terms.
  6. Agent and mapping. Copy this kit's mapping.json into your repository, or openinference.json from the connect-traces skill if your spans follow OpenInference, and create the agent with it: evalkit agents create myagent --trajectory-source otel --mapping my-mapping.json. Do a dry run with your script and evalkit traces check on its session, as in step 2. For each ! line, edit your copy, upload it as a draft and preview the same session:
evalkit traces mapping push myagent my-mapping.json
evalkit traces check myagent <session id> --mapping draft

When it reads right, activate it with the version push printed: evalkit traces mapping activate myagent <version>, or use the agent's Mappings tab in the web UI. Runs always use the active mapping. The connect-traces skill walks a coding agent through the same loop.

SDK runs covers the rest: agents in another process, Python evaluators, and re-scoring. If the evalkit server should drive your agent instead of your script (runs started from the UI, shared agents), implement the Harness API.

docs.title: Next: run evalkit for your team
docs.text: The try-it stack is for one machine. For a server your team shares, follow the evalkit-deployment skill: it covers the server image, Postgres, blob storage, the judge, migrations and the first users and workspaces. A coding agent can walk it with you. Once the server runs, your teammates start from its own /docs page.

docs.title: Stop and clean up
docs.text:
Without Docker: stop evalkit serve with Ctrl-C. To delete everything, drop the database you gave init-server (dropdb evalkit with the default URL) and remove the evalkit-try folder.

With Docker:

docker compose down        # stop; data stays in the volumes
docker compose down -v     # stop and delete all data

docs.title: When something fails
docs.text:
• uv run run.py cannot find evalkit-py==<version>: that version is not on PyPI yet (a source build, or a build whose publish job has not finished). Run it with the wheel you installed instead: uv run --no-project --with "<path to the wheel>[otel]" python run.py, or from an evalkit checkout: uv run --project <checkout> --extra otel python run.py. Or wait for the publish.
  • init-server cannot connect: start Postgres (brew services start postgresql@17, sudo systemctl start postgresql, or Postgres.app), or pass --database-url with the user and password your Postgres needs, e.g. postgresql+psycopg://me:secret@localhost:5432/evalkit.
  • init-server says config.yaml exists: you already set up that folder. Run evalkit serve there, or pass --force to write it again.
  • evalkit serve says a variable is not set: check .env beside config.yaml.
  • Compose says a variable is not set: fill in .env (copied from .env.example).
  • Compose cannot find evalkit:try: outside a checkout, set EVALKIT_IMAGE; in a checkout, add --build.
  • The server will not start: docker compose logs server (and check that .env is filled in: the server reads the LLM settings at start).
  • The server exits with code 132 and no logs (Apple Silicon): the image is older than 0.22.0. Add OPENSSL_armcap: "0" to the server's environment: in docker-compose.yml, or use a newer image.
  • The judge fails on every case: your endpoint must support structured output (response_format with a JSON schema). Try another model.
  • evalkit or run.py talks to another server: run the evalkit login above again, or check EVALKIT_SERVER_URL.

docs.title: Where runs happen
docs.text:
Every dataset and agent lives in a workspace:

  • Personal workspace: one per user, named after the username. Only the owner writes to it.
  • Shared workspace: created by an admin, e.g. dev and prod. Members with the writer role write to it; reviewers approve its cases.
  • Who can read: every logged-in user can read every workspace, including other users' personal workspaces: datasets, cases, experiments, runs, trajectories, spans and sessions, and fixtures. Only the owner writes to a personal workspace; admins and writers write to a shared one. The web UI marks someone else's personal workspace "read-only".
  • Traces are visible too: traces you import or export into your personal workspace, such as production traces pulled for case mining, can be read by everyone on the server. No workspace setting keeps them private. If traces hold data some users must not see, scrub it in your agent before export, or run a separate evalkit server for those traces. A mapping's exclude_spans does not help here: the server stores spans as received and only skips them when it builds a trajectory.
  • Promotion: an admin can link two shared workspaces (evalkit workspaces promote-to dev prod). Approving a case in finance@dev then adds that version to finance@prod, approved, with its overlays. prod is fed only by promotion: sync and review decisions there are refused, comments allowed. Create each target dataset once with evalkit datasets create finance@prod. One target per source, one source per target.

The agent you pick decides who drives the run. The dataset and the agent together decide where the experiment is stored:

  • Both shared: the experiment lives in the dataset's workspace.
  • Otherwise: it lives in your personal workspace.

Example with workspaces @alice (personal), @dev and @prod (shared). myagent is alice's personal agent; ouragent is the team's deployed agent, with one entry per shared workspace.

# Who / entry Dataset Agent Driver Agent runs on Trajectory from Experiment in Use case 1 alice, SDK run_experiment(dataset="finance", agent="myagent") finance@alice myagent@alice (code-driven) alice's Python laptop, in-process OTel → collector → server builds ATIF @alice EDD inner loop (default) 2 alice, evalkit run finance --agent myagent finance@alice myagent@alice (localhost harness) alice's CLI laptop harness ATIF → CLI → server @alice a Harness API agent on this machine 3 alice, evalkit run finance@prod --agent myagent finance@prod (approved only) myagent@alice alice's CLI laptop harness ATIF → CLI → server @alice does a local change break the released set 4 alice, evalkit run finance --agent ouragent@dev finance@alice ouragent@dev server dev cluster harness ATIF or OTel @alice try new cases on the deployed dev agent 5 anyone, UI or run finance@dev --agent ouragent@dev finance@dev ouragent@dev server dev cluster harness ATIF or OTel @dev regression after a deploy or merge 6 anyone, run finance@dev --agent ouragent@prod finance@dev ouragent@prod server prod cluster harness ATIF or OTel @dev does prod pass cases approved in dev 7 anyone, UI or run finance@prod --agent ouragent@prod finance@prod ouragent@prod server prod cluster harness ATIF or OTel @prod release gate 8 deployed ouragent with an agent token none ouragent@prod none prod cluster OTel → collector, browsed in Runs none trajectory debugging of deployed traffic (optional) ✗ anyone, server or UI, --agent myagent@alice any myagent@alice refused the server cannot reach a laptop ✗ bob, --agent myagent@alice any myagent@alice refused only the owner runs a personal agent

docs.title: Example setup: personal → dev → prod
docs.text:
A common setup with two shared workspaces, one per deployed environment of your agent:

  • Personal workspaces: each developer writes and runs cases in their own workspace, on their laptop.
  • @dev: a PR adds or changes cases in the repo. On merge, CI syncs them into @dev. Reviewers of @dev approve them there.
  • @prod: the promotion target of @dev. Approving a case in @dev copies that version into @prod, already approved. Nothing else writes cases to @prod, so it always holds the released set.
@alice ──PR merged, CI syncs──▶ @dev (Unreviewed) ──reviewer approves──▶ @dev (Approved) ──promotion──▶ @prod (Approved)

docs.title: Set it up
docs.text:
An admin runs these once:

evalkit users add alice                                 # prompts for a password; once per user
evalkit users add bob
evalkit workspaces create dev
evalkit workspaces create prod
evalkit workspaces promote-to dev prod                  # approvals in @dev land in @prod
evalkit workspaces members add dev alice --role writer  # may sync and run in @dev
evalkit workspaces members add dev bob --role reviewer  # may approve cases in @dev
evalkit datasets create finance@prod                    # once per dataset, before its first approval

Then:

  1. Set up CI to lint cases on every PR and sync them into @dev on merge. See CI sync.
  2. If the server drives your deployed agent, register it once per workspace, pointing each at that environment's deployment: evalkit agents create ouragent --workspace dev --harness-url … and the same with --workspace prod.

docs.title: Day to day
docs.text:
1. Write and try a case. Alice adds finance/net-debt.yaml and runs it against her own agent: evalkit run finance --agent myagent. This syncs the directory into finance@alice and runs it there.
  2. Open a PR. CI runs evalkit lint on the cases and fails on errors.
  3. Merge. CI runs evalkit sync into finance@dev. The new case is Unreviewed.
  4. Review. Alice asks for a review: evalkit review request finance@dev --case-id net-debt --reviewer bob. Bob approves it: evalkit review approve finance@dev net-debt. He can approve several at once (evalkit review approve finance@dev net-debt fx-rate) or every case waiting on him (evalkit review approve finance@dev --all-waiting). To ask a question first: evalkit review comment finance@dev net-debt --comment "which fiscal year?"; resolve it later by its id: evalkit review resolve 12. evalkit review queue finance@dev lists what is waiting in one dataset.
  5. Promotion. The approval adds that version of the case to finance@prod, approved.
  6. Run. finance@dev holds every merged case, for regression runs after a merge. finance@prod holds the approved ones, for the release gate (rows 5 and 7 in the table above).

Changing a case starts the loop again. The new version is Unreviewed in @dev, and @prod keeps the old approved version until the new one is approved.

A change to a case that is waiting for review, or was sent back with changes requested, goes back to the same reviewer on sync: you don't need to run review request again. If you do, cases already waiting on that reviewer are left as they are.

docs.title: Several branches
docs.text:
• evalkit run syncs the dataset directory first. The dataset in your workspace then matches whichever branch ran last, and the dataset page shows that sync's branch and sha.
  • An experiment pins its case versions when it starts. A sync from another branch never changes a running or finished experiment. Cases removed by that sync are soft-removed, and pinned versions remain.
  • Fixture bytes are content-addressed, so two branches never overwrite each other's bytes under the same key.
  • --resume does not sync, and runs the pinned versions, so it is safe from any branch.
  • Agent config is one row per agent, not per branch.

docs.title: SDK reference
docs.text: The Python SDK runs experiments from your own code. Install it with the otel extra at your server's version (see Install) and import from evalkit.sdk. SDK runs walks through it.

docs.title: run_experiment
docs.text:
run_experiment(
    *,
    dataset: str,
    agent: str,
    task: Task,
    workspace: str | None = None,
    evaluators: Sequence[PythonEvaluator] = (),
    repetitions: int = 1,
    concurrency: int | None = None,
    case_ids: Sequence[str] | None = None,
    tags: Sequence[str] | None = None,
    model: str | None = None,
    resume: int | None = None,
    dry_run: bool | int = False,
    trajectory_wait_seconds: int | None = None,
    judge: JudgeSettings | None = None,
    evaluation_concurrency: int = EVALUATION_CONCURRENCY,
) -> ExperimentResult

Run an experiment: call task once per case and repetition, store the runs on the server and score them.

Scoring uses the judge, the remote evaluators of the agent's workspace and the Python evaluators you pass. Reads evalkit.yaml (cases, fixtures, credentials) from the current directory or a parent, and the login from evalkit login.

Parameters:

  • dataset (str) –

    The dataset to run. A bare name means your personal workspace; if it is also a directory under cases in evalkit.yaml, it is synced first. name@workspace runs a shared dataset, every review state included.

  • agent (str) –

    The code-driven agent on the server that the runs belong to, created once with evalkit agents create. A bare name means your personal workspace.

  • task (Task) –

    Your function, called once per case and repetition, sync or async. Its parameters bind by name from input (the case input), files (list[Fixture]), model and metadata (session_id, experiment_id, case_id, repetition, tags). A task with one parameter of another name receives the input. Return a str (the answer), a dict (the structured output) or a RunResult. A task that raises records a failed run.

  • workspace (str | None, default: None ) –

    The workspace of dataset when it is a bare name.

  • evaluators (Sequence[PythonEvaluator], default: () ) –

    Python evaluators made with evaluator. A case selects one by name under evaluators.custom, like an HTTP evaluator.

  • repetitions (int, default: 1 ) –

    How many times each case runs.

  • concurrency (int | None, default: None ) –

    How many tasks run at once. Defaults to the agent's max_concurrent_runs.

  • case_ids (Sequence[str] | None, default: None ) –

    Run only these cases.

  • tags (Sequence[str] | None, default: None ) –

    Run only the cases carrying any of these tags.

  • model (str | None, default: None ) –

    Passed to the task's model parameter and recorded on the experiment.

  • resume (int | None, default: None ) –

    An experiment id to resume: runs only the cases it has not finished.

  • dry_run (bool | int, default: False ) –

    True runs one case without creating an experiment and prints the answer and what the server made of the session; an int runs that many.

  • trajectory_wait_seconds (int | None, default: None ) –

    How long to wait for a run's spans to settle into a trajectory. Defaults to the agent's setting.

  • judge (JudgeSettings | None, default: None ) –

    The judge for LLM-graded built-in evaluators. Defaults to the server's default judge. Judge(provider=...) names an LLM provider configured on the server: they run on the server with its stored key. Judge(base_url=..., api_key=...) brings your own judge: they run on this machine. The key is never stored.

  • evaluation_concurrency (int, default: EVALUATION_CONCURRENCY ) –

    How many runs are scored at once.

Returns:

  • ExperimentResult –

    The experiment id, its URL and one summary per run.

Raises:

  • RuntimeError –

    When called from a running event loop; await arun_experiment there instead.

docs.text:
evaluate_experiment(
    *,
    experiment_id: int,
    evaluators: Sequence[PythonEvaluator] = (),
    refetch_trajectories: bool = False,
    evaluation_concurrency: int = EVALUATION_CONCURRENCY,
    judge: JudgeSettings | None = None,
) -> ExperimentResult

Re-score an experiment that used Python evaluators.

evalkit evaluate refuses such experiments, because the evaluators live in your script; call this from the script instead. Exported as evaluate_experiment.

Parameters:

  • experiment_id (int) –

    The experiment to re-score.

  • evaluators (Sequence[PythonEvaluator], default: () ) –

    The Python evaluators the experiment ran with. Each must have been part of the experiment.

  • refetch_trajectories (bool, default: False ) –

    Read the trajectories of runs whose trajectory was partial or unavailable again before scoring.

  • evaluation_concurrency (int, default: EVALUATION_CONCURRENCY ) –

    How many runs are scored at once.

  • judge (JudgeSettings | None, default: None ) –

    The experiment's judge again, for an experiment that brought its own (Judge(base_url=..., api_key=...)): keys are never stored, so re-scoring asks for it again. It must be the judge the experiment recorded; a different judge is refused.

Returns:

  • ExperimentResult –

    The experiment id, its URL and one summary per run.

Raises:

  • RuntimeError –

    When called from a running event loop; await aevaluate_experiment there instead.

docs.title: register
docs.text:
register(
    agent: str, only: SpanFilter | None = None
) -> None

Send this process's OpenTelemetry spans to the evalkit server.

Adds an exporter to the global tracer provider, or creates one when none is set. Call it after your own tracing setup, so it joins your provider. Spans go to the server you logged in to (or EVALKIT_SERVER_URL) with the agent token in EVALKIT_OTEL_TOKEN (evalkit tokens create --agent <agent>); a person's login is not accepted, because it expires under a long-running process. Needs the otel extra.

Parameters:

  • agent (str) –

    The agent the spans belong to, e.g. myagent or myagent@dev.

  • only (SpanFilter | None, default: None ) –

    Export only the spans this function returns True for.

docs.text:
evaluator(fn: Callable[..., Any]) -> PythonEvaluator

evaluator(
    *,
    name: str | None = None,
    kind: Kind = "evaluator",
    requires_trajectory: bool = False,

Turn a function into a Python evaluator for run_experiment.

Use it bare (@evaluator) or with options (@evaluator(name=...)). The function receives the same EvalCase and EvalRun the Custom Evaluator API sends: the case id, input, expected block and this evaluator's config from the case YAML (case.config); the answer, structured output and ATIF trajectory as a dict. It returns a float, a ScoreItem, or a list of them.

Parameters:

  • fn (Callable[..., Any] | None, default: None ) –

    The function, when used bare.

  • name (str | None, default: None ) –

    The name cases use under evaluators.custom. Defaults to the function's name.

  • kind (Kind, default: 'evaluator' ) –

    evaluator for a score, gauge for a measurement.

  • requires_trajectory (bool, default: False ) –

    Skip runs that have no trajectory.

Returns:

  • PythonEvaluator | Callable[[Callable[..., Any]], PythonEvaluator] –

    The evaluator, or a decorator that makes one.

docs.title: Judge
docs.text:
The LLM judge an experiment uses; exported from evalkit.sdk as Judge.

Set exactly one of provider or base_url. With provider, the judge is served by an LLM provider configured on the evalkit server: judge-using built-in evaluators run on the server with its stored key. With base_url, you bring your own judge: those evaluators run on your machine, with api_key.

Attributes:

  • provider (str | None) –

    The name of an LLM provider configured on the server.

  • base_url (str | None) –

    An OpenAI-compatible endpoint that supports structured output.

  • api_key (str | None) –

    The key for base_url. Sent only to base_url; never stored on the evalkit server or shown.

  • model (str) –

    The model name at that endpoint.

  • reasoning_effort (str) –

    Passed to the model as reasoning_effort.

  • max_tokens (int) –

    The most tokens one judge reply may use.

  • experiment_id (int | None) –

    The experiment, or None after a dry run.

  • url (str | None) –

    The experiment's page in the web UI, or None after a dry run.

  • runs (list[RunSummary]) –

docs.text:
One run of an experiment.

Attributes:

  • case_id (str) –

    The case.

  • repetition (int) –

    1 for the first repetition, 2 for the second, and so on.

  • status (str) –

    completed, failed, cancelled or timeout.

  • trajectory_status (str | None) –

    valid, partial, invalid or unavailable, or None when no trajectory was read.

    The session the run's spans belong to.

docs.title: evalkit
docs.text:
By InferEdge.

Make your AI agent better, end to end.

evalkit is a self-hosted system for improving AI agents. Real traffic goes in; a better agent comes out, with evals your domain experts signed off on.

TL;DR Mine failures from your agent's real runs and turn them into eval cases. Your domain experts review the cases in plain language, so "right" means what the business means. Run them, read every trajectory, and get file-cited fixes for your prompts, tools and skills. Apply, re-run, repeat until green. Your coding agent drives the loop with evalkit's skills; evalkit keeps the cases, reviews, runs and history.

flowchart LR
  T["Your agent's<br/>real runs"] -->|mine| C["New cases"]
  C -->|review| R["Approved cases"]
  R -->|run| S["Scores +<br/>trajectories"]
  S -->|diagnose| F["File-cited fixes"]
  F -->|apply| A["Better agent"]
  A -->|re-run| S
  A -.->|new runs| T

docs.title: How evalkit improves your agent
docs.text:
1. Find what goes wrong. Pull a batch of your agent's app runs from production, staging or manual testing. Your coding agent analyzes each one, groups the failure patterns and drafts eval cases.
  2. Agree on what right looks like. Domain experts read each case as a question and the facts a right answer must contain, then approve it, comment, or send it back with changes. Approved cases are promoted to your production suite.
  3. Measure it. evalkit runs the cases against your agent, keeps the full trajectory of every run (messages, reasoning, tool calls, tokens, cost, timing) and scores it with LLM-judged rubrics, built-in tool-call checks and your own evaluators.
  4. Fix it. Your coding agent pulls the failed runs, diagnoses each one, and proposes fixes that name the prompt, tool description, skill or data source to change.
  5. Prove it. Apply the fixes, re-run, and compare the two experiments case by case with evalkit summary <new-id> --baseline <old-id>: what got fixed, what broke. The cases stay as regression guards for every change after.

Steps 1, 4 and 5 run as agent skills (evalkit skills install) in Claude Code or another coding agent. Alongside them are skills for writing cases with a domain expert and connecting your traces.

docs.title: Developers and domain experts, one loop
docs.text:
An agent is only as good as the definition of "right" it is tested against. Developers know the prompts, tools and harness; domain experts know what a correct answer is. evalkit gives each side its own view of the same cases.

  • Cases in plain language. A case is a question plus rubrics, one sentence each: "States 17,133 company-operated stores at FY2021 year-end." An expert can read and judge it without reading code. The case-authoring skill interviews the expert in their own terms and writes the YAML.
  • Review in the web UI. Unreviewed → Review requested → Approved, or Changes requested with a comment. Threaded comments sit on the case, and each case keeps a changelog of every sync and decision. Review never filters a run: every case runs, and approval decides which version is promoted.
  • Workspaces. Each developer has a personal workspace to iterate in without touching anyone's results. Shared workspaces such as dev and prod hold the team's datasets, agents and experiments, with writer and reviewer members.
  • Promotion. Link dev to prod, and approving a case in dev copies that exact version into prod. Your prod suite only ever holds reviewed cases.

docs.title: It's that simple
docs.text:
# eval/cases/smoke/cases.yaml
cases:
  - id: store-count
    input:
      question: "How many company-operated stores did Starbucks have at FY2021 year-end?"
    evaluators:
      output:
        answer_rubrics:
          rubrics:
            - rubric: "States 17,133 company-operated stores at FY2021 year-end."
              type: factual_retrieval

# eval/run.py
from evalkit.sdk import run_experiment, tracing
from myagent import ask

tracing.register(agent="myagent")  # your agent's spans become its trajectory


def task(input: dict) -> str:
    return ask(input["question"])


result = run_experiment(dataset="smoke", agent="myagent", task=task)
print(result.url)  # the scorecard in the web UI

docs.title: Why evalkit
docs.text:
• Failures you can read. Open a low score and see exactly what the agent did, step by step.
  • Plug in your traces. Already emitting OpenTelemetry spans with OpenInference or GenAI conventions? evalkit maps them into trajectories. Any harness, any model.
  • See your app runs too. Browse your agent's real runs with their latency, tokens, cost and tool calls, not just eval runs.
  • Graders you choose. Any OpenAI-compatible model as the judge, run by the server or with your own key, and your own evaluators in Python or over HTTP.
  • Cases are code. They live in your repository and sync from CI, like the rest of your code.

docs.title: Run your own evalkit
docs.text:
1. Try it locally. With Python 3.12 or newer, pip install "evalkit-py[server]", then evalkit init-server against a local Postgres, or use Docker. Try locally starts the server on your machine, judges with your LLM, and runs a sample agent through an SDK run with traces.
  2. Deploy it for your team. The evalkit-deployment skill covers the server image, Postgres, blob storage, the judge, migrations, users and workspaces. Config and deploy has the config reference and the compose setup.
  3. Connect your agent.
  4. SDK runs with Tracing and Mappings: the default path.
  5. Harness API: when the server should drive your agent.

docs.text: If your team already runs a server, open its /docs page: the same pages, with your server's URL filled in. Start with the Quickstart.
